Brahma-परिणाम-vāda
(‘the doctrine that ब्रह्मन् transforms itself [into this world]’)
------------------------------------------
The origin of this world, in which we live and move, is one of the important topics invariably discussed in the darśanas or the Indian philosophical systems. The Vedāntic systems, while agreeing that ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute, is the ultimate cause of this world, are not unanimous about the way of evolution of the world from ब्रह्मन्. While the Advaita system describes ब्रह्मन् as the unchanging reality and hence, the world as only an illusory appearance foisted on it due to इग्नोरन्चे of its real nature, the Viśiṣṭā-द्वैत system accepts that ब्रह्मन् does transform itself as this world even as milk becomes curds. (pariṇāma = transformation).
Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta accepts ब्रह्मन् (or ईश्वर) as the primary reality and cit (the sentient beings, the jīvas or the individual souls) as well as अचित् (the insentient nature, also called प्रकृति) as secondary realities dependent on ब्रह्मन्. ब्रह्मन् includes them in itself as an integral part, pervades them and transcends them. It is this अचित् or प्रकृति part that really gets transformed.
This doctrine which accepts that ब्रह्मन् transforms itself into this world through its प्रकृति-part is known as ‘Brahma-परिणाम-वाद’.

brahmacarya
(‘conduct pertaining to ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
One of the words used extensively in the Hindu religious literature is the word ‘brahmacarya.’
Etymologically speaking, the word can mean two things: ‘Movement (caryā) in ब्रह्मन्.’ ‘Code of conduct (caryā) (to be observed during the period of studying the) वेदस् (Brahman).’
When a Vedic student was learning the वेदस् in the होउसे of his preceptor, he had to lead a very strict life, wherein celibacy or continence was the most important discipline. Hence the word ‘brahmacarya’ is, more commonly, interpreted as celibacy.
Celibacy centres round the control and the ultimate sublimation of the sexual instinct. Sex, again, is an instinct of the body. Hence, the best solution to the problems created by the sex-instinct is transcending the body-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् itself and rising to the सोउल्-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. This becomes possible only when the मिन्द् dwells constantly on ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute, to such an extent that the body is forgotten. Hence the very first meaning given is, perhaps, more accurate and includes the latter too.
Of the four stages of life, technically called the ‘āśramas,’ the first is known as the ‘brahmacaryāśrama’ or just ‘brahmacarya;’ and the student undergoing it is called a ‘brahmacārin’.
A ब्रह्मचारिन् entered the गुरुकुल or the होउसे of the preceptor for studying the वेदस् as also other sciences, after undergoing the sacrament of उपनयन. The period of this ब्रह्मचर्य was usually twelve years, though it could be more.
The following are some of the rules and discipline that a ब्रह्मचारिन् was expected to observe: strict celibacy, speaking the truth, gentleness in speech, physical austerities like cold water bath, eating sparingly at night and service to the preceptor, devotion to study and contemplation.
He was to beg his ड़ोओद् and could partake of it only after offering it to the preceptor.
Though ब्रह्मचर्य or celibacy was obligatory for the brahmacārins and the saṁnyāsins (monks), even the householders were advised to observe it as best as they could.
See also ĀŚRAMA and UPANAYANA.

Brahmāṇī
(‘the spouse of ब्रह्मा’)
------------------------------------------
According to the शक्ति-cult or the cult of the Divine मोथेर्, each one of the major gods of the Hindu pantheon has his शक्ति or power, portrayed as the female consort or counterpart, with a similar form, weapons and vehicle. ब्रह्माणी, also known as ब्राह्मी, is the शक्ति of ब्रह्मा, the four-faced god of च्रेअतिओन्.
According to the Durgāsaptaśatī, one of the basic texts of the शक्ति-cult, when Kauśikī दुर्गा was fighting the demon Raktabīja—whose blood, if spilled, could produce demons similar to him—she manifested out of herself seven emanations. These are usually called the सप्तमातृकास् or ‘Seven little Mothers’. ब्राह्मी or ब्रह्माणी is the first among them.
According to the Matsyapurāṇa when ब्रह्मा was in deep meditation, his pure body divided itself into two halves—male and female—and the female deity came to be known as ब्रह्माणी, सावित्री, सरस्वती and Īatarūpā.
Iconographical works describe her as having four faces and six arms. Her colour is piṅgala or tawny. She wears a deerskin as an upper garment. She holds the rosary and a wooden spoon (sruva) as also a book and a water pot in four hands. The other two hands display the abhaya and the varada mudrās, signifying the giving of protection and boons asked for. She rides on a swan.

Brahma-sarovara
(‘lake of ब्रह्मा’)
------------------------------------------
Kurukṣetra, where the महाभारत war, between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kauravas, is said to have been fought, is a famous place of पिल्ग्रिमगे even now. It is situated in the Karnal-Ambala region of Haryana, about 40 kms. (26 miles) to the east of the Ambala city.
According to the पुराणस् it was surrounded by five lakes called ‘Samantapañcaka.’ One of these lakes, the biggest, is called Brahmasarovara or Brahmasaras. Since it is situated in the present कुरु-क्षेत्र region, it is commonly known as the कुरुक्षेत्र lake. It is also called Pavanahrada. It is 1320 meters (4400 ft.) long and 640 meters (2100 ft.) wide.
Brahmā, the creator, is said to have had his yūpasthambha or the sacrificial pillar here. Hence the name ‘Brahma-sarovara.’ king कुरु, from whom the race of the Kurus originated, is said to have performed तपस् here.
There are two small islands inside this lake containing an ancient temple of विष्णु and the ruins of some old temples.
Taking a bath in this lake, especially during the solar एच्लिप्से, is considered to be extremely auspicious. Great merit also accrues to those who circumambulate it.
See also KURUKṢETRA.

Brāhmī
(‘that which is related to ब्रह्मा’)
------------------------------------------
Brāhmī is the शक्ति or power of ब्रह्मा, the creator, considered as his consort. See BRAHMĀṆĪ for details.
Brāhmī is also the name of a script, one of the earliest in recorded history, and, considered as the मोथेर् of the देवनागरी script as also the allied scripts, like those of Tibet, Burma, Sri Lanka and Thailand.
The earliest records available in the ब्राह्मी script are the edicts of अशोक. Most of them, except the ones found in the North-West part of India, are in the ब्राह्मी script. The North-Western edicts are in the खरोष्ठी script.
The ब्राह्मी is normally read from left to right.
Regarding its origin there are two theories. Most Indian scholars maintain that it was derived from the Harappan script. Many European scholars believe that it was derived from a Semitic script like the Greek, Aramaic or the Phoenician.
The Hindu tradition holds that it has come from ब्रह्मा, the Creator, himself; and hence the name ब्राह्मी. The similarities with the script of Indus valley civilization seem to support the theory of its Indian origin.
But, one thing is certain: By the time of emperor अशोक (272-232 B.C.) the script was not only in existence but had also been considerably developed and refined.
Knowledge of the script had long been forgotten. It goes to the credit of James Prinsep (A.
-1840) and Kamalākānta Vidyālaṅkāra for the complete decipherment of the script in A.

.
See also KHAROṢṬHĪ.

Brahmaṇaspati
(‘lord of ब्रह्मन् [prayer or the वेदस्]’)
------------------------------------------
‘Brahmaṇaspati’ is one of the names that occurs in the Ṛgveda as also in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. He may be the deity of prayer and of the text of the Veda itself. He is said to control the clouds and rain and help the world by protecting vegetation.
Scholars differ as regards his exact identity. He is identified with several roles: अग्नि (the fire-god), the priest of god इन्द्र, deity of vegetation and hence a form of चन्द्र or the मोओन् and so on.
There is reason to believe that ब्रह्मणस्पति is another name for बृहस्पति, the preceptor of the gods.
See also BṚHASPATI.

Brahmopaniṣad
------------------------------------------
The Brahmopaniṣad is a minor Upaniṣad and is assigned to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. There seems to be two recensions—the South Indian and the North Indian. The latter is the longer version.
Śaunaka approaches the sage Pippa-lāda of the अङ्गिरस्-गोत्र and puts him a question regarding the location and functioning of the deities of the इन्द्रियस् or sense-organs in the divine ब्रह्मपुर (the human body). In reply, पिप्पलाद imparts the excellent ब्रह्मविद्या or spiritual wisdom concerning आत्मन्/ ब्रह्मन्.
It is प्राण or आत्मन् that exercises its power over all the देवस् or the इन्द्रियस् (sense-organs). Situated in this Brahma-pura (the human body) it is the pure, resplendent, partless ब्रह्मन् that controls these sense-organs.
When the जीव (prāṇa or आत्मन्) goes out of the body during सुषुप्ति or deep sleep, all the sense-organs also follow him even as the bees follow the queen bee. He moves about in sleep like an eagle flying freely in the sky. In this state of सुषुप्ति the जीव is not tainted or affected by good and bad. He comes back to the waking state through the dream state.
This पुरुष (the जीव or the आत्मन् bound in this body) has four seats where his presence is felt: नाभि (navel), हृदय (heart), kaṇṭha (throat) and mūrdhā (head). Associated with the four states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, viz., जाग्रत् (waking state), स्वप्न (dream state), सुषुप्ति (deep sleep state) and तुरीय (the fourth or the super-conscious state), he is known respectively as ब्रह्मा, विष्णु, रुद्र and अक्षर. But in himself he is pure Light, beyond the limitations of all the sense-organs.
At the cosmic level, since he is everything and all things are merged in him without distinction, the worlds, the gods, the sacrificial systems, all human relationships and varieties of human beings do not exist separately as distinguished from him.
The Upaniṣad then goes on to describe the real meaning of śikhā (tuft of hair) and यज्ञोपवीत (sacred thread) as related to ब्रह्मन् (the Absolute). The externals should be discarded and ज्ञान or knowledge (of the आत्मन्) should take their place.
This is then followed by some verses which appear in other उपनिषद्स् like the Śvetāśvatara also. They describe the Supreme Lord as the all-pervading reality and also as residing in the hearts of all beings in a subtle form. He is the supreme witness, energiser, master-controller and supervisor. Those who realize him in their own hearts attain eternal happiness, and not the others.
Just as the fire which is inherent in the araṇis (attritional pieces of wood used in वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् to produce fire) is brought out by their attrition, or oil from the oil-seeds or butter from curds or water from the earth by proper means, the आत्मन् inside us can be brought out, i.e., experienced, through meditation. Once this is done, the जीव or the individual सोउल् is liberated from all types of bondage.
See also UPANIṢADS.

brahmahatyā
(‘the slaying of a ब्राह्मण’)
------------------------------------------
Though man is essentially divine in nature, he is prone to vice and committing crimes, thus incurring पातक or पाप or sin. This is mainly due to the evil tendencies carried over from the past lives.
Etymologically, the word पाप (sin) is defined as ‘that from which one has to protect oneself’. It arises first in the मिन्द् as the tendency towards vice and manifests itself either in neglecting the prescribed duties or in committing prohibited actions. The scriptures are the primary, if not the sole, authority in this field.
The dharmaśāstras—the works that deal with the religio-social life of the Hindus—have classified sins into two major groups: the महापातकस् or atipātakas (major or mortal sins) and upapātakas (minor or venial sins).
Brahmahatyā or the killing of a saintly ब्राह्मण, is one of the महापातकस् that is often mentioned in these works. Any act that will lead either indirectly or directly to the slaying of a ब्राह्मण is ब्रह्महत्या. Even incitement or approval is liable to be branded as ब्रह्महत्या. And it entails unbearable suffering.
One does not incur ब्रह्महत्या if one kills a ब्राह्मण who is an ātatāyin (a criminal guilty of grave offences), in self-defence.
With regard to its expiation, there does not seem to be any unanimity among the writers of these works. It ranges from death, up to undergoing severe austerities like offering one’s limbs into fire, walking very long distances with very little or no ड़ोओद्, performing sacrifices like अश्वमेध or अभिजित् or Gosava and so on.
See also PĀPA, PRĀYAŚCITTA and PUṆYA.

brahmarandhra
(‘the crevice of ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
The crevice in the crown of the head is called ‘brahmarandhra’ since ब्रह्मन् (Īśvara or God) is said to have entered this body through this randhra or crevice, after creating it, to make it alive (vide ऐतरेय Upaniṣad

Brahmāstra
(‘the missile of ब्रह्मा’)
------------------------------------------
The art and science of warfare was highly developed in ancient India, if the accounts of war given in the Rāmāyaṇa and the Mahābhārata are to be believed.
Weapons used were divided into two broad categories: astras and śastras. Astras were missiles discharged from their sources like the bow. Śastras were weapons used by directly holding them in hand. Arrows, discuses and spears belong to the first, whereas swords belong to the second category.
By far, the most powerful of all the astras often mentioned in the epics and the mythological lore is the ब्रह्मास्त्र also called ‘Brahmaśirostra’. शिव is said to have given it to the sage अगस्त्य. अगस्त्य gave it to अग्निवेश who gave it to Droṇa. अर्जुन got it from Droṇa.
According to another version, ब्रह्मा the creator specially made it for Devendra. The sage अगस्त्य who got it in course of time, handed it over to Śrī राम.
It is more likely that the ब्रह्मास्त्र was not a particular missile physically existent, but a terrible power that could be invoked into any missile by the appropriate mantras. Its use was restric-ted to extraordinary situations and when the enemy was not an ordinary human being.
Śrī राम is reputed to have killed रावण with this ब्रह्मास्त्र.

Brahmāṇdapurāṇa
(‘the mythological work that deals with the Cosmic Egg’)
------------------------------------------
The पुराणस् or the mythological scriptures have played, over the centuries, a very constructive and effective role in educating the Hindu masses. These masses had been denied direct access to the study and knowledge of the वेदस् and allied scriptures. However, the need for enlightening them not only in moral and spiritual values but also in certain aspects of secular एदुचतिओन्, including vocational training, had been keenly felt by the sages and the pragmatic sections of the society. And, the पुराणस् fulfilled that need admirably.
The Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa is the last of the eighteen major पुराणस् (mahā-पुराणस्). It is called so, probably because, it deals with the ब्रह्माण्ड, the world and its च्रेअतिओन्, as a major subject. Hindu tradition attributes its authorship to the sage व्यास. It was perhaps composed near the place where the river गोदावरी rises (near Nasik of Maharashtra). Generally considered as one of the oldest of the eighteen पुराणस्, it might be assigned to the period A.

-400.
Since a major part of this purāṇa agrees with the Vāyupurāṇa, some scholars are inclined to think that the two were originally a single work and later split into two due to cult rivalries.
The work as available in print now, comprises four pādas as follows: Prakriyā (5 chapters), Anuṣaṅga (33 chapters), Upodghāta (74 chapters) and Upasaṁhāra (4 chapters). Thus, the 12,000 verses of this purāṇa are spread over 116 chapters in 4 pādas. This is followed by Lalitopā-khyāna (in 40 chapters) which contains the famous Lalitāsahasranāma, a hymn known for its mystical power and is extremely popular in South India.
The subjects dealt with in this purāṇa may be summarised briefly as follows: च्रेअतिओन्, geography of the earth and of भारतवर्ष, manvantaras, pupils of व्यास and the distribution of the Vedaśākhas or branches of the वेदस्; च्रेअतिओन् of gods, demons, गन्धर्वस्, sages and their progeny; all aspects of śrāddha or obsequial ceremonies in detail; exploits of the warrior-sage परशुराम; story of the descent of the river गङ्गा to this earth; धन्वन्तरि and the आयुर्वेद, the science of health and longevity.
The writers of the धर्मशास्त्रस् have quoted verses from this purāṇa fairly extensively in support of their views.
See also PURĀṆAS.

brahmotsava
(‘the big festival’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu temples and worship of the images permanently fixed in their गर्भगृह (sanctum sanctorum) are quite ancient. Out of the several public festivals observed by these temples, the ‘brahmot-sava’ is the biggest. (‘Brahma’ means ‘big’.) However, the orthodox belief is that the fourfaced ब्रह्मा (the creator-god) himself conducts this festival in honour of the chief deity of the temple. Hence the name ‘brahmotsava’. Generally it is the grandest and the most spectacular of all the temple-festivals. The celebrity of a temple is often measured by the extent of the grandeur of its ब्रह्मोत्सव.
Āgāmic works speak of five varieties of brahmotsavas. They are:
brāhma : It is celebrated just for a day and is supposed to increase the spiritual power of the temple.
śaiva : It is conducted for three days and is aimed at removing all the obstacles of the people.
aindra : Spread over five days, this is believed to prevent famine and drought.
ārṣa : Conducted for seven days, this is meant to secure prosperity for the kingdom.
daivika or vaiṣṇava : This is a nine-day affair purported to bring about all-round protection and happiness.
This last one is considered as sāttvika (pure) as against the others which are either rājasika (middling) or tāmasika (inferior).
Some of the more important aspects of a ब्रह्मोत्सव are: bherītāḍana (beating the drum), dhvajārohaṇa (hoisting the temple flag), आवाहन (inviting the deity to the yāgaśālā or place of sacrificial rites), establishing of kalaśas (holy pots filled with water) and performance of homas.
The रथोत्सव (festival of taking the उत्सवमूर्ति or the procession-image in the रथ or temple car) is conducted two days before the close of the festival.
In some temples where there is the facility of a tank or a river nearby, teppotsava or boat-festival too is celebrated.

brāhmī-sthiti
(‘the state of being established in ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
Brahman is the Absolute from which this universe has evolved, in which it lives and to which it returns at the end of a cycle of च्रेअतिओन्. It is described as ‘sat-cit-आनन्द,’ existence-knowledge-bliss absolute.
When a person, through appropriate sādhanās or spiritual practices, realises this ब्रह्मन् in the inmost depths of his being, his life undergoes a dramatic change, reflecting this inner experience in every action. Such a person called ‘sthitaprajña’ or ‘a man of steady wisdom’, always maintains an equanimous attitude towards all situations of life.
This inner state of mystical experience resulting from realising ब्रह्मन् and expressing itself outwardly as equanimity has been called ‘brāhmī-sthiti’ by the Bhagavadgītā (2.72). Once attained, this state will continue till the last moment of one’s life.

Brāhma-mantra
(‘mantra connected with ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
Mantras are mystic syllabus or formulae supposed to be endowed with supernatural powers. According to some tāntrik works, mantras can be classified into two groups: the Saguṇa-mantras and the Brāhma-mantras.
The former are connected with the Saguṇa ब्रह्मन् (Brahman with attri-butes) and the latter with the Nirguṇa ब्रह्मन् (Brahman without attributes). Whereas upāsanā or meditation with the former leads to savikalpa-समाधि (samādhi in which the मिन्द् takes the form of the deity and results in its reali-zation), upāsanā with the latter results in निर्विकल्प-समाधि (samādhi in which the formless ब्रह्मन् is experienced).
The well-known महावाक्यस् (‘great sentences’) culled from the उपनिषद्स् chosen from the four वेदस् are classed under Brāhma-mantras. The number of the Brāhma-mantras may vary from 12 to 1,80,000. The गायत्री-मन्त्र has been described as the best of the Brāhma-mantras.

brahmodya
(‘that which stimulates [a knowledge of] ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
During the ancient days performance of the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् was widely prevalent. Though the sacrifices took a lot of time to do them meticulously, intervals and free time would also be there. These had to be utilised in a way useful to the people involved, especially the priests. One such programme that served this purpose well was the ‘brahmodya,’ a theological dialogue, where questions and riddles were propounded and answered. This helped the priests and others to enrich their knowledge in the company of persons endowed with better knowledge and greater experience. A sample of the same, which occurs in the अश्वमेध sacrifice may be given here: pṛcchāmi paramantaḥ pṛthivyāḥ, .....iyaṁ vediḥ paro antaḥ, ‘I ask you the furthest limit of the earth.....’ ‘This वेदि is the furthest limit.’ (Ṛgveda 1.164.34,35)

brahmarṣi
(‘knower of ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
A ṛṣi is one who has known the truth (ṛṣ = to know) or attained the final goal (ṛṣ = to attain) of life. Of the seven types of ṛṣis mentioned in the Hindu religious works, the ब्रह्मर्षि stands as the first or the highest in eminence. He has known or experienced ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute, the Self of all, and has thus reached the other end of सṁसार or transmigratory existence.
If the word ‘Brahman’ is interpreted as the वेदस्, then, the ब्रह्मर्षि is one who has obtained a thorough knowledge of the वेदस्.
The sages like शुक, सनक, Sanandana and वसिष्ठ are classed among the brahmarṣis.
See also ṚṢI.

Brāhmanism
(‘Religion of ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
Scholars from the Western countries who got interested in the study of हिन्दुइस्म् during the 19th century and the early part of the 20th century, used the words ‘Brāhmanism,’ ‘Brāhminism’ and ‘Vedism’ to indicate हिन्दुइस्म्. Since God, the Absolute, has been designated as ‘Brahman’ they used the word ‘Brāhma-nism’. Since, according to them, it was a religion practised and propagated by the brāhmaṇas—members of the first of the four varṇas—it was also called ‘Brāhmi-nism’. Again, the वेदस् being the main and basic scriptures, the appellation ‘Vedism’ was also used.
However, a deeper and wider study of all aspects of हिन्दुइस्म् clearly reveals the deficiency of these terms in indicating हिन्दुइस्म्.

Brahmā
------------------------------------------
Broadly speaking, Hindus can be divided into three main groups: Śaivas or those who worship शिव, Śāktas or those who worship शक्ति (consort of शिव) and Vaiṣṇavas or those who worship विष्णु. However, popular Hindu theology, which has its roots in the ancient scriptures, adds another important deity, ब्रह्मा. The three—Brahmā, विष्णु and Śiva—together form the Hindu Trinity.
Brahmā creates the world, विष्णु sustains it and शिव destroys it. This process of च्रेअतिओन् (sṛṣṭi), preservation (sthiti) and destruction (pralaya) continues perpetually in that order.
Thus ब्रह्मा is the source, the seed, of all that is. He is, as his very name indicates, boundless immensity, from which space, time and causation originate, names and forms spring up. Philosophically, he is the first stage of manifestation of the notion of individual existence (ahaṅkāra). Theologically, he is the uncreated Creator (Svayambhū), the self-born first Person.
He has several designations which are as instructive as they are interesting. From the cosmological point of view, he is the Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha), the ball of fire, from which the universe develops. Since all created beings are his progeny, he is प्रजापति, the Lord of progeny, as also the Pitāmaha, the Patriarch. He is विधि, the ordinator, Lokeśa, the master of the worlds, as well as Dhātṛ, the sustainer. He is also Viśvakarmā, the architect of the world.
Hindu mythological literature des-cribes ब्रह्मा as having sprung from the lotus originating from the navel of विष्णु. Hence he is called Nābhija (the navel-born), Kañja (waterborn) and so on.
Curiously enough, the name ‘Nārā-yaṇa’ (‘the one who dwells in the casual waters’ or ‘the abode of man’) has been applied to him first and later only to विष्णु.
Brahmā, the creator and सरस्वती, his consort, are the subjects of several tales in our mythological literature. They can be summarised briefly thus:
Brahmā was born out of the golden egg produced in the boundless causal waters. His consort Vāc or सरस्वती was manifested out of him. From their union were born all the creatures of the world.
Brahmā represents the वेदस् and सरस्वती, their spirit and meaning. Hence all knowledge, sacred and secular, has proceeded from them.
Once ब्रह्मा became the boar and raised the earth from beneath the waters and created the world, the sages and प्रजापति.
The forms of tortoise and fish, (later considered as avatāras of विष्णु) have been attributed to ब्रह्मा also.
The great sages मरीचि, अत्रि, अङ्गिरस् and others are his ‘mind-born’ children. मनु, the Adam of the Āryan race, is his great-grandson.
He is easily pleased with auster-ities and bestows boons on the supplicants, be they gods, demons or human beings.
He is the inventor of the theatrical art. मुसिच्, dance and stagecraft were revealed by him.
He was the chief priest who per-formed the मर्रिअगे of पार्वती with शिव.
In spite of the fact that ब्रह्मा is God the Supreme in the creative aspect and is an equally important member of the Hindu Trinity, it is strange that there are no temples dedicated exclusively to him, the one at Puṣkar (near Ajmer in Rajasthan) being the solitary exception. Notwithstanding the crude reasons given in some of the पुराणस् for the loss of ब्रह्मा’s prestige, it is likely that the ब्रह्मा cult was predominant in the pre-Vedic हिन्दुइस्म् and was superseded by the later शिव-विष्णु cults. In fact, the evolution of the शक्ति concept—each of the gods शिव and विष्णु having his शक्ति or Power as his consort—and the explanation that च्रेअतिओन् proceeds from the combination of the God and his शक्ति, has made ब्रह्मा superfluous.
The icon of ब्रह्मा has four heads facing the four quarters, and they represent the four वेदस्, the four युगस् (epochs of time), and the four varṇas (divisions of society based on nature, nurture and vocation). Usually the faces have beards and the eyes are closed in mediation. There are four arms holding different objects and in different poses. The arms represent the four quarters. The objects usually shown are: अक्षमाला (rosary), कूर्च (a brush of कुश grass), sruk (ladle), sruva (spoon), कमण्डलु (waterpot) and पुस्तक (book). The combination and arrangement vary from image to image.
The rosary represents time and the waterpot, the causal waters, from which all च्रेअतिओन् has sprung up. So, ब्रह्मा controls time as well as the principle of causation. The कुश grass, the ladle and the spoon being sacrificial implements, represent the system of sacrifices which is the means to be adopted by the various creatures to sustain one another. The book stands for knowledge, sacred and secular. He is the giver of all knowledge—arts, sciences and wisdom.
The mudrās or poses of the hand are abhaya (assuring protection) and varada (granting boons).
The icon may be either in the standing posture (standing on a lotus) or in the sitting posture (sitting on a हṁस or swan). हṁस or the swan stands for discrimination and wisdom.
In the temples dedicated exclusively to ब्रह्मा, his aspect as विश्वकर्म (the architect of the universe) is adopted. In this form he is shown as having four heads, four arms holding the rosary, the book, the कुश grass and the कमण्डलु and riding on his swan.
Every temple, be it of शिव or विष्णु, must have a niche in the northern wall for ब्रह्मा, and his icon must receive worship everyday since he is an important parivāradevatā (attendant of the Chief deity).
Brahmā is also the name applied to one of the four principal priests in a Vedic sacrifice. He is the most learned of all and is required to know the three वेदस् for his professional duties. He acts as a presiding officer of a sacrifice and is silent most of the time. He instructs the अध्वर्यु priest when his advice is sought for. It is he who prescribes the prāyaścittas (expiatory rites) when mistakes are committed in a sacrifice.
In later Vedic literature, he came to be associated with the Atharvaveda.

brahmanāḍī
(‘the nāḍī or passage [that leads to] ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
According to the works on हठयोग and राजयोग, कुण्डलिनी-शक्ति, the basic energy of a human being, lies dormant like a coiled serpent, at the base of the spinal column in the मूलाधार-चक्र. When roused by proper yogic practices, it crawls up the सुषुम्ना-nāḍī, the central passage for its flow, encased inside the spinal column and reaches the सहस्रार-चक्र at the crown of the head. There it gets merged in शिव, the Supreme Lord, thus giving enlightenment and bliss to the योगि.
Inside the सुषुम्ना-nāḍī, there are three more nāḍīs—vajriṇī, citriṇī and brahmanāḍī—concentric, one inside the other. ब्रह्मनाडी is the inmost of them stretching from the मूलाधार to the pericarp of the सहस्रार.
Since the जीव (individual सोउल्) attains ब्रह्मन् (God, the Supreme) by raising his कुण्डलिनी-शक्ति through this nāḍī, it is called ब्रह्मनाडी.
See also CAKRAS and NĀḌĪS.

Brahma-mīmāṁsā
(‘enquiry into the [nature of] ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
See BRAHMASŪTRAS.

brahmaśilā
(‘the stone of ब्रह्मा’)
------------------------------------------
Hindu temples are built as per the instructions given in the आगमस्. The गर्भगृह or the sanctum sanctorum is the heart of the temple structure. The icon of the deity is placed in the centre of this. Below the icon, several objects are placed one above the other, starting with the आधारशिला (base stone). Over this are placed a pot, tortoise and lotus made of stone, two more tortoises and lotuses made of silver and gold and a funnel shaped tube called ‘yoganālā’ above which the slab ब्रह्मशिला is placed. The ब्रह्मशिला will be at the floor level. The icon is placed over this ब्रह्मशिला.

brahmāṇḍa-dāna
(‘gift of ब्रह्माण्ड or egg of ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
Giving gifts has always been consi-dered as a sacred act, helping the donor to destroy his sins or to attain higher worlds after death or to get any other result he desires. The Hindu धर्म-śāstras have listed certain gifts, as mahādānas or great gifts. They may be ten as per some works and sixteen as per others. ब्रह्माण्ड-दान is one of them. It consists in gifting to a worthy ब्राह्मण, two pans of gold (to represent the dome of हेअवेन् above and the earth below) of specified dimensions and with the figures of the eight दिग्गजस् (mythical elephants guarding the eight quarters), the लोकपालस् (rulers of the various worlds and of ब्रह्मा in the middle of them.
See also BRAHMĀṆḌA and DĀNA.

Brahmagītā
(‘Song of ब्रह्मा’)
------------------------------------------
The Mahābhārata, considered as the ‘Pañcama-veda’ or the fifth Veda, has enriched human life as also itself by bequeathing the Bhagavadgītā to the posterity. However, the same epic also contains several other pieces of religious discourses, each one of them with a different name, but with word ‘gītā’ affixed to it. Of the sixteen such gītās, the Brahmagītā also is one. It comprises just nine verses, from the 4th to 12th verse, in chapter 35 of the Anuśāsanaparva.
In the course of his long discourse to युधिष्ठिर, the eldest of the Pāṇḍava princes, भीष्म, the grandsire, narrates how in the beginning of this cycle of च्रेअतिओन् ब्रह्मा, the Creator, brought forth the four varṇas or classes of human beings—the ब्राह्मणस्, the kṣattriyas, the vaiśyas and the śūdras—and taught them wisdom.
The ब्राह्मणस् were advised to live a life of self-control, to study the वेदस् with devotion, to offer sacrifices to the gods in हेअवेन् and not to hurt any being. They could get whatever they wanted, just by तपस् (austerity) and ज्ञान (know-ledge). He also exhorted them to never stoop to performing the works meant for the शूद्रस्. That would degrade them spiritually.
Since धर्म was preserved by such ब्राह्मणस्, he counselled the other three classes to protect and serve the ब्राह्मणस्.
Because this teaching was delivered by ब्रह्मा, it has been named as the Brahmagītā.
There is a Brahmagītā in the Sūtasaṁhitā which itself is a part of the Skāndapurāṇa. See SŪTASAṀHITĀ for details.

brahmasūtra
(‘the thread of ब्रह्मा’)
------------------------------------------
The cult of शिव and the worship of his emblem, the लिङ्ग, are as old as हिन्दुइस्म् itself. The liṅgas installed in temples are almost always made of stone. They consist of three parts out of which only the third part—called ‘Rudrabhāga’—is seen above the ground. This cylindrical portion alone—termed ‘pūjābhāga’—is to be worshipped. It contains certain lines technically called ‘brahmasūtra,’ without which the लिङ्ग becomes unfit for worship.
See also ŚIVALIṄGA.

brahmavidyā
(‘knowledge of ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
The words ब्रह्मन् and आत्मन् are extensively used in the Hindu scriptures.
The word ‘Brahman’ has several senses: God the Absolute, the वेदस्, a ब्राह्मण, the ब्रह्मा-priest in a Vedic sacrifice as also तपस् or austerity. However, it is in the first sense that it is more widely used.
Vidyā means knowledge, wisdom, an art or a science. Hence ब्रह्मविद्या refers to that art or science or discipline by practising which, one is able to attain ब्रह्मन् or God the Absolute.
This ब्रह्मविद्या is very ancient and has a hoary tradition. According to the उपनिषद्स्, ब्रह्मा, the Creator, was himself the first teacher. It has been handed down to us by a galaxy of successive teachers.
One who aspires for ब्रह्मविद्या should first cultivate the sādhana-catuṣṭaya or the fourfold spiritual discipline, like विवेक (discrimination) and वैराग्य (renunciation). (See also SĀDHANACATUṢṬAYA for details.) तपस् (austerity) and devotion to the spiritual preceptor are other aspects of this discipline.
The teacher of ब्रह्मविद्या should be a श्रोत्रिय (well-versed in the scriptures) and a brahmaniṣṭha (established in ब्रह्मन्). It is obligatory on his part to impart that knowledge to one qualified for it, if he requests for the same.
The word ‘brahmavidyā’ is sometimes applied to the knowledge of the वेदस् and their subsidiary sciences, since वेदस् are also known as ब्रह्मन्.
See also BRAHMAN and UPANIṢADS.

brahmacārin
(‘a student of the वेदस्’)
------------------------------------------
See BRAHMACARYA.

Brahman
(‘that which is big or great’)
------------------------------------------
One of the most widely used terms in the Hindu religious literature, the word ‘Brahman’ has several senses: the वेदस्, hymns of praise, a priest, one of the four principal priests in a sacrifice representing the Atharvaveda, a ब्राह्मण, तपस् or austerity, God the Creator (the four-faced ब्रह्मा) and the Supreme Spirit or the Absolute. However it is in the last sense that it is extensively used, and hence needs greater explanation.
An oft-occurring theme in the उपनिषद्स् is the assumption and search for the unity in diversity. ‘What is that, by knowing which, everything else is known?’—is a typical question that is raised in them (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad.
; Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. 4.5.6; Chāndogya Upaniṣad

). The sages of the उपनिषद्स् realized in the depths of their mystical experience, that there was a basic reality underlying the entire universe of multiplicity, the One without a second, and called it ‘Brahman’.
The word ‘Brahman’ is derived from the root ‘bṛh’ (‘to grow,’ ‘to burst forth’) and hence means that which is immense and that from which everything else has come out. In other words, it is from ब्रह्मन् that this world has evolved, it is in ब्रह्मन् that it rests even after this evolution and again, it is to that ब्रह्मन् that it returns at the time of involution. ‘Sṛṣṭi,’ ‘sthiti’ and ‘laya’ or ‘pralaya’ are the three words generally used to indicate these processes. ब्रह्मन्, however, remains unaffected by this evolution or involution and is ever full and perfect (pūrṇa) in itself.
The intrinsic power of ब्रह्मन् with which it creates this world, sustains it and withdraws it into itself, is called ‘māyā’.
Since च्रेअतिओन् is only an evolution of Brahman—which evolution is considered as only apparent and not real, according to some schools of Vedānta—Brahman continues to exist in it as the immanent reality. Thus it is both transcendent and immanent simultaneously.
Quite often, the उपनिषद्स् use the word ‘Ātman’ as synonymous with ब्रह्मन्. Sat, अक्षर and Bhūmā are some of the other terms used to indicate ब्रह्मन्.
The evolution of the world from the ब्रह्मन्/Ātman is generally traced as follows: From the ब्रह्मन् evolves आकाश (ether); from आकाश comes वायु (wind) from वायु comes अग्नि (fire), from अग्नि comes ap (water) and from ap comes pṛthivī (earth). Vegetation and then, life (including the human beings) evolve out of this earth.
In the Vedāntic works based on the उपनिषद्स्, four aspects of ब्रह्मन् have been put forth: the Absolute called ब्रह्मन्, the creative spirit ईश्वर (Lord, God), the world-spirit हिरण्यगर्भ and the world, विराज्.
The totality of च्रेअतिओन् which is none other than ब्रह्मन् in essence, is the विराज्. When ब्रह्मन् is thought of as the spirit moving everywhere in the world, it is called हिरण्यगर्भ. When conceived as the personal God engaged in the act of च्रेअतिओन्, protection and destruction of the world, it is called ईश्वर. When believed to be established in itself independent of any च्रेअतिओन्, it is ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute.
The Reality is not a sum of these. It is an ineffable unity in which these conceptual distinctions are made.
Brahman, the Absolute, is unique and different from all that we know and experience here. Hence it can be predicated only in negative terms, ‘neti, नेति,’ ‘not this, not this’. This should not mislead us into thinking that it is a non-entity. While it is non-empirical, it is also inclusive of the whole empirical world. And, it has an essential nature of its own: ‘sat’ or being, ‘cit’ or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and ‘ānanda’ or bliss. These are not its characteristics but are different phrases for the same being: self-being, self-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and self-delight.
There are also passages in the उपनिषद्स् that describe ब्रह्मन् as पुरुष or the Supreme Being. He is the Aupaniṣada-पुरुष, the Being described in the उपनिषद्स् and known only through them. He is the Hiraṇmaya-पुरुष, the golden Being, the Supreme सोउल् existing in the आदित्य or the sun (vide Bṛhadāraṇyaka
; Chāndogya
), He is the Mahān-पुरुष, the great Person, by knowing whom one can transcend death (Śvetāśvatara
). He is greater than the greatest and smaller than the smallest (Kaṭha
). He has pervaded everything and has established himself as the inmost Self in all the beings (Īśāvasya
Up. 1
; Kaṭha
). He is the Lord of the lords and God of the gods. There is none that is superior to him or even his equal (Śvetāśvatara
-9). He bestows boons on his devotees that worship him (Kaṭha

).
The Vedāntic schools of Rāmānuja (A.
-1137) and Madhva (A.
-1317) identify ब्रह्मन् with विष्णु/ नारायण.

Brahmapurāṇa
(‘the purāṇa [revealed by] ब्रह्मा’)
------------------------------------------
The religious practices of the modern Hindus depend largely upon the information and instruction given by the paurāṇic literature. This literature has grown voluminously over several centuries.
Hindu tradition recognises 18 mahā-पुराणस् or major पुराणस् and 18 upa-पुराणस् or subsidiary ones. The Brahma-purāṇa (also spelt as Brāhmapurāṇa) is invariably placed at the head of the list of the major पुराणस्. It is sometimes called the Ādipurāṇa or the Ādibrahma-purāṇa. It may have attained its present form by the 10th to the 12th century A.D. It gets its name mainly due to the fact that ब्रह्मा narrates it, even though व्यास is the narrator in the later part. It may have originated in the गोदावरी basin.
The Brahmapurāṇa, as available in print now, has 13,783 verses, spread over 245 chapters.
The contents, which deal with various aspects of Hindu religion may be presented briefly as follows: च्रेअतिओन् of the world and the living beings, histories of various kings, description of the earth with its seven islands, hells of various types, दक्ष’s sacrifice and its destruction by शिव, detailed descriptions of various places of पिल्ग्रिमगे like Ekāmra, Avantī and Puruṣottamakṣetra (Purī), origin of the river गङ्गा, story of रावण, story of the king हरिश्चन्द्र, story of Śrī कृष्ण in detail, various avatāras or incarnations of विष्णु, performance of śrāddhas or obsequial rites, spiritual wisdom contained in Sāṅkhya and योग darśanas, and a eulogy of listening to the whole purāṇa.
Its treatment of the places of पिल्ग्रिमगे is fairly exhaustive and its verses on this subject have been extensively quoted by the writers on the धर्मशास्त्रस्.
See also PURĀṆAS.

brahmayajña
(‘sacrifice unto ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
Every गृहस्थ or householder was expected to perform five yajñas or sacrifices everyday. They were called ‘pañcamahāyajñas’. They had nothing to do with the śrauta or the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् wherein oblations had to be poured into the duly consecrated Vedic fires, but were of the nature of performing certain obligatory duties.
Brahmayajña is one of them. Here, Brahma means the वेदस् and ब्रह्मयज्ञ means recitation of the Vedic texts as prescribed by the धर्मशास्त्रस्.
In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (11.5.6. 3-8) there is an interesting comparison of the various limbs and functions of the body involved in reciting the वेदस्, with the implements used in a sacrifice. For instance, the various spoons and ladles like जुहू, upabhṛt and dhruvā are symboli-cally represented by the speech, the मिन्द् and the eyes. The conclusion of the Vedic chanting in the ब्रह्मयज्ञ is अवभृथ-स्नान or the ceremonial bath at the end of a sacrifice.
Brahmayajña may be performed either in a quiet place outside the village or in one’s own होउसे. The usual practice is to do it during the सन्ध्या or at noon. After sitting on the seat and performing आचमन (ceremonial sipping of water) certain prescribed Vedic texts are to be chanted. Generally, it is one’s own branch of the Veda studied in the गुरुकुल. Other works mentioned for स्वाध्याय (self-study) during ब्रह्मयज्ञ are: the four वेदस्, the ब्राह्मणस्, the Kalpas, the itihāsas and पुराणस्.
The contents of the ब्रह्मयज्ञ varies from one śākhā (branch of the वेदस्) to another. However, the गायत्री-मन्त्र, the Puruṣasūkta and the śānti-मन्त्र ‘Oṁ namo brahmaṇe....’ seem to find a place in almost all these traditions.
Now-a-days, ब्रह्मयज्ञ is rarely performed. However, during the lunar month of Śrāvaṇa (July-August) it is performed once by most ब्राह्मणस्, especially in South India. A set formula has been adopted which includes the गायत्री-मन्त्र, the Ṛgveda (

-9), the first sentences of Aitareya Āraṇyaka, the Kṛṣṇa and Śukla Yajurvedas, the Sāmaveda, the Atharvaveda as also the first sentences of the six वेदाङ्गस्. This is followed by the śāntimantra ‘Oṁ namo brahmaṇe’ and a तर्पण (water libation).
See also PAÑCA-MAHĀ-YAJÑAS.

Brahmasūtras
(‘aphorisms [dealing with] ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
Preamble—Sūtras
The system of एदुचतिओन् in ancient India required the students to live in the campus of a forest academy along with the teachers. The teaching imparted was, almost always, in the form of sūtras or aphorisms, followed by explanations and discussions. At a time when committing things to memory was considered supremely important, this method suited admirably.
The sūtra literature is a class by itself. As per the norms set for a sūtra, it should be ‘alpākṣara’ (consisting of minimum number of letters), ‘asandigdha’ (without doubt as regards the meaning), ‘sāravat’ (must contain the essence of the subject) and yet ‘viśvatomukham’ (reflect all aspects of the same). However, in their anxiety to economise the words, the composers of the sūtra-works seem to have so overdone it that bhāṣyas or explanatory commentaries by later writers became necessary.
The śrauta, the gṛhya and the धर्म sūtras form the earliest bunch of sūtra literature. The darśanas or the philosophical systems which are of a later period, followed this sūtra model since it served their purpose well.
Vedānta Darśana
Out of the six darśanas or systems of philosophy which accept the authority of the वेदस् (the basic scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्), the last two—the Mīmāṁsā and the Vedānta systems—are directly connected with them. Whereas the former tries to reconcile the various Vedic texts that seem to give different directions with regard to the same ritual system, the latter attempts to make out a coherent philosophy of ब्रह्मन् (God, the Absolute) from the apparently conflicting statements in the उपनिषद्स्.
Prasthānatraya
The Vedānta system, as its very name implies, deals with the उपनिषद्स् which are the end-portions (anta = end) of the वेदस् and also contain the essence (anta = core or essence) of the same. The system itself is based on three canonical works: the उपनिषद्स्, the Brahmasūtras and the Bhagavadgītā. The उपनिषद्स् are called ‘śrutiprasthāna’, the Brahmasūtras, ‘nyāyaprasthāna’ and the Bhagavadgītā, ‘smṛtiprasthāna’, the three together being termed ‘prasthānatraya’. ‘Prasthāna’ means a school of philosophy or religion.
The Upaniṣads
Though a very large number of works going by the name ‘Upaniṣad’ are available in print today, orthodox tradition accepts only a handful of them—twelve to fourteen—as ancient and authoritative. The entire edifice of the Vedānta system of philosophy depends upon these few उपनिषद्स्.
The teachings of the उपनिषद्स् may, broadly speaking, be classified as follows: ब्रह्मन् as the ultimate cause of this world, nature of ब्रह्मन्, evolution of this world and its character, nature of the living being as individual souls, their relationship with ब्रह्मन्, their involvement in this world as well as their transmigration, the final goal of life, the disciplines that help in reaching that goal and the nature of attainment of that final goal.
It is a fact that the उपनिषद्स्, as extant today, do not give a coherent picture of these various subjects discussed in them. Since tradition and orthodoxy deem the entire body of the उपनिषद्स् as one canonical scripture—the Śruti—it became necessary to reinterpret and reorganise their teachings so as to give them a more coherent look. It was exactly this that बादरायण attempted and the result was the Brahmasūtras.
The Brahmasūtras
The work derives its name from the fact that it deals chiefly with ब्रह्मन् (God, the Absolute) as described in the उपनिषद्स्, in all its aspects. It is also known by other names as follows:
The Vedāntasūtras, since the subject matter is that of Vedānta or the उपनिषद्स्;
The Śārīrakasūtras, since the आत्मन् living in the śarīra or the body is dealt with in the work;
The Uttaramīmāṁsāsūtras (as opposed to the Pūrvamīmāṁsāsūtras) since it does mīmāṁsā or enquiry into the uttara or latter part of the वेदस्;
The Bhikṣusūtras since it is specially recommended for study by the bhikṣus or the saṁnyāsins.
Bādarāyaṇa, the Author
Nothing is known about बादरायण, the author of this celebrated work. Tradi-tionalists identify him with व्यास, the author of the Mahābhārata and the पुराणस्. The work is generally assigned to the period 500 B. C.-200 B. C. by the Indian and some Western scholars. However there are other scholars who consider the two to be different and assign बादरायण to the period A.

.
About the Work
The work Brahmasūtras is in four adhyāyas or chapters. Each adhyāya is divided into four pādas or quarters. The pādas comprise adhikaraṇas or topics, each composed of sūtras.
The total number of adhikaraṇas and sūtras, according to शङ्कर, the earliest commentator, are 191 and 555 respectively. However, variations are seen in this number as also in the readings themselves. Splitting one sūtra into two, fusing two sūtras into one or adding the last word of a sūtra to the beginning of the next are some of the reasons for such variations in the readings. Such alterations in the structure of the sūtras have contributed to divergent interpretations also. Not only that, divergent views have also arisen due to one school considering a particular sūtra as stating the पूर्वपक्ष (the prima facie view, the objection or doubt) and another school accepting the same sūtra as the सिद्धान्त (the theory propounded by the author of the work).
As already stated, each pāda of the various adhyāyas, comprises several adhikaraṇas or topics. An अधिकरण needs must have five parts connected in a graded manner. They are:
viṣaya or topic;
viśaya or saṁ-śaya, doubt;
pūrvapakṣa or opponent’s view;
siddhānta or established conclusion and
saṅgati or connection between the different sections.
The number of sūtras in any अधिकरण depends on the nature of the subject under discussion. Thanks to the ambiguity in the sūtras, the titles and the number of the adhikaraṇas vary from commentator to commentator.
While निम्बार्क (13th century A.D.) has the minimum number of adhikaraṇas (151), Madhuvā (A.

-1317) has the maximum (223).
The purport of the sūtra itself is determined by the commentators as per the principle of षड्विधलिङ्गस् or six characteristic signs. They are: उपक्रम and upasaṁhāra (the beginning and the end), अभ्यास (repetition), apūrvatā (novelty), phala (objective), अर्थवाद (eulogy) and upapatti (logicality).
True to its name, the work Brahma-sūtras, deals primarily with ब्रह्मन् as the highest truth, by realising which, a person transcends transmigratory existence. The one and only authority for the existence of ब्रह्मन् as also for its true nature is the śruti, the jñanakāṇḍa part (section dealing with the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्/ आत्मन्) of the वेदस्, comprising the उपनिषद्स्. This knowledge of ब्रह्मन् can never be obtained by लोगिच् and reasoning which depend upon the puny human intellect. Since the intellect depends upon the knowledge gained by the senses and since ब्रह्मन्, the pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् that he is, is beyond the ken of the senses, the śruti as revealed to the ṛṣis is the only source for knowing him.
This takes us to the next point—the various Upaniṣadic statements that form the basis for the philosophy of the Brahma-sūtras. Since some of these statements appeared to contradict one another, Bāda-rāyaṇa had to undertake the unenviable task of collating them to weave out a homogeneous philosophy. While doing it, he naturally chose the most ancient of the उपनिषद्स्. Which are those उपनिषद्स् the statements of which, बादरायण has discussed in these sūtras? There is no direct indication in the sūtras themselves since they are too laconic. For this we have to depend almost entirely on the bhāṣyakāras or the commentators who, fortunately for us, are more or less unanimous in deciphering the same.
In the first 31 adhikaraṇas (as per शङ्कर) the major statements that form the viṣaya or viṣayavākya (subject matter) are from the following उपनिषद्स्, with the number of such sentences noted against them:
Chāndogya (14), Bṛhadāraṇyaka (5), Kaṭha (4), Taittirīya (2), Muṇḍaka (3), Praśna (1) and Kauṣītaki(2).
Apart from these, sentences taken from the Śvetāśvatara, the Aitareya and the Jābāla have also been discussed.
While analysing the purport of the various passages from the उपनिषद्स्, बादरायण has quoted the opinions of other teachers also. They are: आत्रेय, Āśmarathya, Auḍulomi, Kārṣṇājani, Kāśa-kṛtsna, जैमिनि and Bādari. Almost all these names appear in the earlier works like the śrauta-sūtras and the गृह्यसूत्रस्. It is likely that some preceded बादरायण and others like जैमिनि might have been his contemporaries. Though he differed from them, he has not criticised their views, probably because they were also Vedāntins of repute, who had accepted the उपनिषद्स् as the primary authority and ब्रह्मन् as the highest Truth.
A Brief Synopsis
The contents of the work may now be summarised as follows:
First Chapter
The first chapter comprising 134 sūtras in 39 adhikaraṇas has been called Samanvayādhyāya, (samanvaya = harmony) since it attempts to harmonise the principles dealt with in the various उपनिषद्स्.
The work starts with the famous sūtra athāto brahmajijñāsā (‘Now, therefore, the desire to know ब्रह्मन्’). Since the knowledge or experience of ब्रह्मन्, leads to मोक्ष or freedom from transmigration, it is very necessary to have a correct understanding of ब्रह्मन्. Keeping this in view, the treatise deals with the various statements in the well-known उपनिषद्स् concerning ब्रह्मन्. ब्रह्मन् is he from whom this world came into existence, in whom it inheres and to whom it returns at the end of a cycle of च्रेअतिओन्. The only source for the knowledge of this ब्रह्मन् is the śruti or the उपनिषद्स्.
It is ब्रह्मन् alone who is the ultimate cause of this world and not प्रकृति or प्रधान as the Sāṅkhyas aver, since it is insentient. An insentient cause can never think or will and produce such a perfectly designed universe.
This ब्रह्मन् is ānandamaya, full of bliss. He is transcendent as well as immanent in this world, including the jīvātmas or the individual souls. The being of light that exists in आदित्य or the Sun and our eyes is also ब्रह्मन्. He is also designated as आकाश, प्राण, bhūmā and अक्षर. The being described as ‘aṅguṣṭha-mātra पुरुष’ (the person of the size of the thumb) is also really ब्रह्मन् and not the जीव or the individual सोउल्. So also does the word आत्मन् refer to him.
Bādarāyaṇa quotes the opinions of Āśmarathya, Auḍulomi and Kāśakṛtsna in the fourth pāda of this chapter. Āśmarathya thinks that the jīvātmas are both different and non-different from ब्रह्मन् (or परमात्मन्) even as the sparks of fire are both identical with and different from fire. Auḍulomi opines that the jīvas are different from ब्रह्मन् in the state of bondage but become one with him in the state of लिबेरतिओन्. Kāśakṛtsna, however, considers the two to be identical since it is ब्रह्मन् that has become the जीव also.
Though the views of these teachers are stated, बादरायण does not give his own opinion or preference.
The last part of this chapter asserts that ब्रह्मन् is both the उपादानकारण (material cause) and the निमित्त कारण (efficient cause) for this world.
Second Chapter
Designated as Avirodhādhyāya, this chapter with 157 sūtras distributed among 47 adhikaraṇas applies itself to dispel any virodha or contradiction that may confront this philosophy of Vedānta.
Vedānta is not opposed to स्मृति (secondary scriptures like the Bhagavad-gītā and Āpastamba Dharmasūtras) and तर्क (logic and reasoning). The opposition of schools like that of Sāṅkhya is fallible. There is no contradiction among the various statements in the उपनिषद्स् dealing with subjects like च्रेअतिओन्. This is the burden of the teaching of this chapter.
Out of the several non-Vedāntic systems of philosophy that existed during बादरायण’s time, the Sāṅkhya system was the most powerful. Hence it has been given special attention while refuting other schools.
One of the important factors discussed here is the relationship between the कारण (the cause) and the कार्य (the effect). The Sāṅkyan view known as ‘Satkāryavāda’ states that the कार्य or the effect pre-exists (sat = existing) in the कारण or cause. In the process of च्रेअतिओन् it just gets manifested and is not newly produced, since something real can never be produced from the unreal. On the other hand the Vaiśeṣika school accepts the ‘asat-कार्य-वाद,’ according to which the previously non-existent (= असत्) effect is newly produced. In the former case, the effect pre-exists in the upādāna-कारण (the material cause) and in the latter, the निमित्त-कारण (the efficient cause) is constant. बादरायण accepts these views partially and declares, on the basis of the उपनिषद्स्, that ब्रह्मन् is ‘abhinna-निमित्त-upādāna-कारण’, both the material and the efficient cause, for this world. Hence this world is non-different from ब्रह्मन्. The objection that this world consists of insentient objects and hence cannot be the product of the sentient ब्रह्मन् does not hold good, since the Śruti, the highest authority in such matters which are beyond the powers of the ordinary human intellect, declares it to be so.
Brahman has no selfish motive in creating this world, since he is self-contented. There is neither partiality nor cruelty in this च्रेअतिओन् since justice is meted out to the jīvas according to their karmas or deserts. The very purpose of च्रेअतिओन् of this world is to help the jīvas to attain आनन्द or bliss by getting established in ब्रह्मन्, the Bliss-Absolute.
Apart from the Sāṅkhya school, the other schools like those of the Vaiśeṣikas, the Buddhists, the Jains, the Pāśupatas and the Bhāgavatas, like the Pañcarātras have also been critically examined and dismissed.
Third Chapter
The third chapter is called Sādhanā-dhyāya and is the longest with 186 sūtras spread over 67 adhikaraṇas. Though called thus, the topics discussed are diverse. They are: transmigration of the जीव into other bodies, dream-creations of the जीव, its experiencing the deserts of कर्म by the will of ईश्वर or God, various विद्यास् or meditations mentioned in the उपनिषद्स् and clarifications regarding them, collating of a विद्या when described differently in different उपनिषद्स्, knowledge of the आत्मन् or ब्रह्मन् as independent of karmas or rituals and duties prescribed for the various āśramas (stages of life like ब्रह्मचर्य or सṁन्यास) as also prāyaś-cittas (expiations) and so on.
Fourth Chapter
Known as Phalādhyāya this chapter is the shortest with only 78 sūtras and 38 adhikaraṇas. The main topic discussed is the journey of the जीव after death to ब्रह्मलोक by the ‘arcirādimārga’ or ‘devayāna’, the path of light or of gods.
One who is interested in मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् has to practise śravaṇa (listening to the scriptures describing the nature of आत्मन् [Brahman] and allied disciplines until realisation). The various upāsanās or meditations described in the उपनिषद्स् aid the जीव in the process of attaining मोक्ष. On attaining ब्रह्मज्ञान or knowledge of ब्रह्मन्, sañcita-कर्म (karma accumulated over several lives) gets destroyed. आगामी-कर्म, कर्म done after realisation is rendered fruitless. The prārabdha-कर्म, the कर्म that has already started this body and yielding the results, has to be exhausted only by experiencing it.
The jīvas who have practised severe spiritual disciplines like तपस् (austerity), श्रद्धा (devoted faith) and ब्रह्मचर्य (celibacy), as also विद्यास् like meditation on ब्रह्मन् will travel, after death, by the arcirādimārga or the path of light comprising light, day, bright fortnight and so on, and reach the ब्रह्मलोक from which there is no return. There are divine guides called ‘ātivāhikās’ who take the जीव through the various stations of light to the ब्रह्मलोक.
Anomalies in the descriptions concerning the details of the arcirādimārga have been set right through proper interpretations and arguments.
The work ends with the declaration, ‘anāvṛttiḥ śabdāt,’ repeated twice for emphasis, (‘There is no return since the scriptures declare so.’) meaning that the जीव reaching ब्रह्मलोक will not return to this mundane existence. Descriptions of the nature of the मुक्तपुरुष, the liberated सोउल्, are given at the appropriate places. The views of जैमिनि, Auḍulomi and Bādari in this regard have also been cited.
The Philosophy of Bādarāyaṇa
Bādarāyaṇa wrote the Brahmasūtras to systematise the teachings of the Upa-niṣads into a coherent philosophy. However, since the sūtras are short and terse, it becomes quite a job to find out what exactly is his own philosophy as revealed through this work. Even so, with the help of the sūtras which seem to be more unambiguous than the others, an attempt may now be made to portray the same.
The one and only pramāṇa (source of knowledge) that बादरायण accepts while expounding the Vedānta system is Śruti or the वेदस्, especially the ज्ञान-kaṇḍa part or it, viz., the उपनिषद्स्. He considers the words of the वेदस् as नित्य or eternal. लोगिच् and reasoning, which can always be unsettled by superior ones, can never be relied upon in determining the transcendental truths like the ultimate Cause of the world. Smṛtis or secondary scriptures like the Manusmṛti and the Mahābhārata including the Bhagavad-gītā can also be depended upon in so far as they do not contradict the Śruti.
The Śruti declares ब्रह्मन् as the origin of this universe, the primary, nay, the only truth. In fact, the very definition (janmādyasya yataḥ,

) makes him the uncaused cause, the ground of sustenance and involution of the world. He is both the material and efficient cause for the world. He needs no external implements or assistance and can transform himself even as milk is transformed into its products.
He evolves himself into आकाश (ether), वायु (air) and other products by willing the same; and, he is associated with every stage of च्रेअतिओन् up to the last.
Since it is ब्रह्मन् that has evolved into this world, this world is non-different from him, even as an unfolded cloth is non-different from the same which was earlier folded.
The activity of च्रेअतिओन् is a līlā or effortless sport for ब्रह्मन्. But, since it is done as per the karmas of the unredeemed jīvas, one should not attribute partiality or cruelty to him, seeing the good and evil that exist here.
As regards the जीव or the individual सोउल्, बादरायण defines him as a ‘jña’ or knower, a being endowed with चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्. He has no birth or death. He is eternal and atomic in size. Whether the जीव is an aṁśa (part) of ब्रह्मन् or his आभास (reflection) has not been stated clearly though the views of other Vedāntins like Āśmarathya, Auḍulomi and Kāśakṛtsna have been given.
The relationship between the जीव and ब्रह्मन् has been likened to the snake and its coiled-up state or light and its source. Thus the question whether they are different or identical has been left unanswered.
By meditation on आत्मन्/Brahman leading to ज्ञान, or experience of the same, the जीव attains लिबेरतिओन्. The Śrutis give equal importance to the perfor-mance of कर्म or prescribed actions and त्याग or renunciation of the same, though the performance of duties prescribed for the respective āśramas (stages of life) has been stressed even for the spiritual aspirant. The fruits of the various upāsanās or meditations practised by a जीव accrue to him by the grace of ईश्वर (Brahman as the ruler of the created world).
On attaining the knowledge of ब्रह्मन् all the sañcita कर्म (accumulated past कर्म) of the जीव will be destroyed. He will live as long as the prārabdha कर्म (karma already fructified) lasts. But, the कर्म does after attaining knowledge will not affect him.
The जीव who has reached the acme of meditation while living, will, after death, travel by the arcirādimārga or देवयान (the path of light or of the gods) and reach ब्रह्मलोक from which there is no return to this world. There, he will be one with ब्रह्मन्, non-different from him. The various attributes predicated of ब्रह्मन् get manifested in the liberated जीव. चैतन्य or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, being his essential nature, is of course, always there.
In conclusion it can be affirmed that बादरायण, in these sūtras, teaches a kind of advaita (Brahmādvaita?).
He does not admit the existence of either the jīvas or the world, as indepen-dent of or different from ब्रह्मन्. Since he has accepted the उपनिषद्स् as the supreme authority and since the other teachers like Bādari whom he has quoted, also did the same, he has not contradicted them. Both the views—that ब्रह्मन् is निर्विशेष-cinmātra-svarūpa (pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् without any attributes) and saviśeṣa (with attributes)—seem to be acceptable to him. Obviously he has tried to reconcile the various, apparently conflicting, views expressed in the उपनिषद्स् and explain them rather than formulate his own philosophy.
The Commentators and their Works
The वेदस् have been the foundation of Hindu religion and culture for millennia. The philosophy of Vedānta based on the उपनिषद्स् has held sway over the intelligentsia for centuries. Hence, it is but natural that the Brahmasūtras of Bāda-rāyaṇa has attracted the attention of the distinguished scholars over the years who have enriched the Vedānta literature by their brilliant expositions. All these commentators have evinced great respect for Bādrāyaṇa and his monumental work. They have tried to critically examine all the other schools that were important during their days and to prove the superiority of the Vedānta over them. Of course, they were equally keen to establish their own school of Vedānta also.
Of the several bhāṣyas or commen-taries available to us today, that of शङ्कर is the earliest. There might have been quite a few bhāṣyas composed by the earlier writers. It can however be stated with certainty that उपवर्ष, to whom शङ्कर refers in his commentary (
