A brief summary of the more important of these schools may now be given. Since the schools propounded by शङ्कर, Rāmānuja and Madhva are more well-known and gained precedence over the others, they will be taken up first.
Śaṅkara
Śaṅkara’s दर्शन or philosophy as revealed in his bhāṣyas on the Bhagavad-gītā, the ten ancient उपनिषद्स् and the Brahmasūtras is now well-known as Advaita Vedānta. The oft-quoted and famous verse ‘brahma satyaṁ jagan मिथ्या jīvo brahmaiva nāparaḥ’ (‘Brahman alone is real; this world is only an illusory appearance. The जीव is verily ब्रह्मन् and is not different from him.’) gives this philosophy in a nutshell.
Śaṅkara categorises ब्रह्मन् into two aspects: पर-ब्रह्मन् and Apara-ब्रह्मन्. Where the Upaniṣadic statements deny all limiting adjuncts like name and form, created by अविद्या or इग्नोरन्चे of his essential nature to ब्रह्मन्, he is पर, the higher, ब्रह्मन्. On the other hand, where these statements describe him as endowed with name, form and several attributes, it is the Apara or the lower, ब्रह्मन् that is referred to. It is the latter that is the cause for the च्रेअतिओन् of this world, its sustenance and its dissolution.
Really speaking, ब्रह्मन् does not get transformed into this world. The multiplicity of names and forms is only a ‘vivarta,’ an appearance, due to अविद्या or इग्नोरन्चे, even as a snake is perceived in a rope in insufficient light. This, he calls as ‘adhyāsa’ or ‘adhyāropa’ (superimposition). Through विद्या or discriminative knowledge, ‘apavāda’ or desuperimposition takes place giving the true knowledge of the reality.
Śaṅkara considers the jīvas as चैतन्य or pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, but, circumscribed by the अन्तःकरण (the ‘inner organ’ or मिन्द्). The जीव, though नित्य (eternal), śuddha (pure), बुद्ध (awakened) and mukta (free), appears as kartā (the doer) and bhoktā (the experiencer) due to the limitations imposed by the अन्तःकरण.
The Upaniṣadic sentences like tat tvam asi teach the essential identity between the जीव and ब्रह्मन्, as pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, after eliminating their adventitious qualities.
Śaṅkara does accept क्रममुक्ति or gradual लिबेरतिओन् of the जीव after death, by travelling through the देवयान, to ब्रह्मलोक, as described in the उपनिषद्स् and the Brahmasūtras. However, he is emphatic about sadyomukti or instant लिबेरतिओन्, here and now, simultaneously with the rising of ज्ञान or knowledge. Such a मुक्ति is also called जीवन्मुक्ति, लिबेरतिओन् even while living.
Rāmānuja
Rāmānuja’s commentary on the Brahmasūtras is known as Śrībhāṣya. Apart from this, he has also composed two more, smaller, works on the Brahma-sūtras, the Vedāntadīpa and the Vedānta-sāra. The former, being a later work, contains some additional explanations.
Rāmānuja’s Śrībhāṣya is stated to follow in the footsteps of the more detailed Bodhāyana-vṛtti as also the works of some earlier Vedāntins like Brahmanandī and Dramiḍācārya whose works are not available now.
Rāmānuja accepts ब्रह्मन् as the highest and independent reality. However ब्रह्मन् includes in himself cit (the sentient beings, the jīvas) and अचित् (the insentient प्रकृति or nature). These two are also real, but under the absolute control of ब्रह्मन्. Brahman—also called ईश्वर by him—includes them, is immanent in them and also transcends them. Hence, Rāmānuja’s system is called ‘Viśiṣṭādvaita,’ advaita or non-duality of ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute, but ‘viśiṣṭa’ or qualified by cit and अचित्. It is similar to a tree with branches, leaves and fruits. Though the tree is ‘one,’ it has internal parts, each part being different from the other parts, the tree itself, however, always remaining as one.
To Rāmānuja, ब्रह्मन् is the Supreme Person (Sarveśvara) who is the ruler of all. He is antagonistic to all evil. He possesses infinite auspicious qualities. He is Omniscient and Omnipotent. The च्रेअतिओन्, subsistence and reabsorption of this world proceed from him.
Rāmānuja considers the जीव or the individual सोउल् as the spirit different from the body, atomic in size and endowed with ज्ञान or चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् which contracts or expands.
He has a free will. And, the jīvas are infinite in number. Some jīvas called ‘nitya’ are ever free. Others who are now ‘baddha’ or bound, can attain मुक्ति through भक्ति and प्रपत्ति (devotion and surrender) and the grace of God. All the liberated jīvas are similar in nature.
Spiritual life starts with the performance of the prescribed karmas in the right spirit leading to the purification of the मिन्द्. Such a pure जीव becomes fit to practise ज्ञान and experience his separateness from the body-मिन्द् complex. However, it is through भक्ति and प्रपत्ति that he ultimately attains ब्रह्मन् through the देवयान and becomes free.
Madhva
A thorough-going dualist, Madhva has composed 37 works which collectively go by the name Sarvamūla. The short and terse bhāṣya on the Brahmasūtras, the Aṇubhāṣya a brief treatise on the same, in verses, Nyāyavivaraṇa and the Anuvyākhyāna are the four works on the sūtraprasthāna. His is a philosophy of realism and a monotheistic theology cente-ring on devotion to विष्णु or नारायण.
According to him ब्रह्मन्, identified with विष्णु (Nārāyaṇa) is the independent reality. प्रकृति or matter and the jīvas or souls who are atomic and infinite in number, are coeval realities but entirely dependent on him. ब्रह्मन् is essentially knowledge and bliss. Though his infinite personality is beyond our conception, out of grace for us, he can take forms which are neither material nor finite.
Madhva proclaims the theory of पञ्चभेदस् or five eternal differences between ब्रह्मन् and the jīvas, ब्रह्मन् and प्रकृति, jīvas and प्रकृति, जीव and जीव and various objects of प्रकृति.
He categorises the jīvas into three groups: मुक्तियोग्यस्, nityasaṁsārins and tamoyogyas. The first group is capable of attaining मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन्. The second group, being interested only in the crass pleasures of the world and not a whit in moral regeneration or spiritual elevation, eternally go through the rounds of births and deaths. The third group, the damned sinners that they are, degenerate into lower births and suffer in हेल्ल्.
The jīvas get लिबेरतिओन् through भक्ति and the grace of God. In the state of लिबेरतिओन् they are not only freed from suffering but also enjoy positive bliss. Differences among the jīvas, however, persist even in the state of लिबेरतिओन्.
Bhāskara
Bhāskara is the trail-blazer for the post-शङ्कर schools of Vedānta which did not agree with शङ्कर’s brand of advaita based on māyāvāda, the theory of the unreality of the world. He is a strict Vedāntin in the sense that he takes his stand on the उपनिषद्स् and the Brahma sūtras. His commentary on the latter expounds his philosophy.
Bhāskara advocates the acceptance of the direct meaning of all the passages of the उपनिषद्स् without distinction. He presents a ब्रह्मन् who has innumerable auspicious attributes, but, without any particular form. He has a twofold power—the bhoktṛśakti (the power of the enjoyer) and the bhogyaśakti (the power of the enjoyed). Using these two powers he transforms himself into the acetana or insentient objects and the jīvas or the sentient souls. Though this transformation is real, it does not affect him in any way. The jīvas in their essential nature are one with ब्रह्मन्, but get differentiated from him in the state of bondage due to the upādhis or limiting adjuncts—the bodies and the minds—which are real. These upādhis, though real, are not नित्य or eternal. They are to be considered as real since they are actually experienced. But, in the state of लिबेरतिओन्, they become one with ब्रह्मन् even as the rivers flowing into the ocean become one with it.
Bhāskara considers this world as the kāryārūpa or effect, of ब्रह्मन्, and hence real.
As regards the sādhana, भास्कर recommends performance of scripture-ordained duties without desire for their fruits and the practice of meditation on ब्रह्मन् as also the जीव’s oneness with him. Since he does not accept a personal God, there is no place for divine grace in his system.
Nimbārka
Nimbārka’s द्वैताद्वैत is very similar to the Bhedābheda of भास्कर. However, being a firm believer in ब्रह्मन् with form and attributes and the path of devotion, his philosophy is more akin to that of Rāmānuja.
Nimbārka’s main work is Vedānta-पारिजात-saurabha which is his commentary on the Brahmasūtras. It is rather brief but lucid, since he avoids the dialectical methods or a flowery style.
According to him there are three equally real and co-eternal tattvas or principles: ब्रह्मन्, cit and अचित्. While ब्रह्मन् is the controller or niyantṛ, cit (the sentient being, the जीव or the souls) is the enjoyer, भोक्तृ and अचित् (the insentient nature, प्रकृति) is the enjoyed, भोग्य.
Acit is of three kinds: prākṛta or what is derived from प्रकृति or primal matter; aprākṛta or what is not derived from a non-material substance of which the world of ब्रह्मन् is made and, kāla or time.
They are different from one another in their svarūpa or nature. But the cit and the अचित् are paratantra-tattvas, dependent realities.
Nimbārka adopts the view that the bheda (difference) and the abheda (non-difference) are both equally real. They co-exist but do not contradict each other. It is something like the relationship between the sea and its waves or the sun and its rays. Cit and अचित्, the souls and the universe, exist in ब्रह्मन् from all eternity and never get separated from him whether in the casual state or when manifested. They retain their individuality even during salvation or dissolution of the universe.
Brahman is personal, possesses a celestial body, full of exquisite beauty and grace. निम्बार्क identifies him with कृष्ण and posits राधा as his शक्ति or consort even as Rāmānuja accepts लक्ष्मी as the consort of विष्णु-नारायण.
Brahman is omniscient, the cause of the origin, sustenance and destruction of the universe. He is all-powerful and yet all-merciful. He is gracious to his devotees and helps them have a direct vision of himself.
The jīvas are atomic and infinite in number. Each of them is a distinctive agent, a jñatṛ (knower), kartṛ (doer) and भोक्तृ (enjoyer) of the karmas he does. They animate the body they live in, even as a small lamp kept in a room lights up the whole room.
There are three destinies for the jīvas—naraka or the हेल्ल् for the sinners, स्वर्ग or हेअवेन् for the virtuous and अपवर्ग or release for enlightened ones. अपवर्ग is attaining the world of ब्रह्मन् from which there is no return.
Constant meditation on ब्रह्मन् as the inmost Self of the जीव or the individual सोउल् is the means of attaining ब्रह्मन् in ब्रह्मलोक. There he has brahma-svarūpa-lābha, becomes similar in nature, except for the power of च्रेअतिओन्.
The other sādhanās recommended are: scripture-ordained work, knowledge, devotion and surrender to God, as also strict obedience to the spiritual teacher.
Vallabha
Vallabha’s philosophy is known as शुद्धाद्वैत. He is said to have written two commentaries on the Brahmasūtras, the Bṛhadbhāṣya and the Aṇubhāṣya, of which the former is not available now. The latter is up to the 33rd sūtra of the second pāda of the third adhyāya (

). The book was completed by his son Viṭṭhalanātha. Apart from the प्रस्थानत्रय, he holds the Bhāgavata in very high esteem. He wrote a commentary on it also, called Subodhinī, which too remained incomplete.
For वल्लभ, God the Absolute is कृष्ण whom the उपनिषद्स् call ‘Brahman’. He is one without a second and is sat-cit-आनन्द, (being, awareness and bliss). He has three forms: परब्रह्मन्, पुरुषोत्तम or कृष्ण; अन्तर्यामिन्, the indwelling spirit of all the living beings and अक्षर-ब्रह्मन् which is the object of meditation and the abode of कृष्ण. It is this अक्षर that appears as प्रकृति (insentient nature, the matrix of all created objects) and पुरुष (sentient सोउल्, the जीव), but is beyond both. While पुरुषोत्तम is the highest, अक्षर is an expression of his.
This अक्षर, again, appears in three more forms: kāla (time), कर्म (action) and svabhāva (nature).
Kāla or time is suprasensible and is inferred from its effects. It is all-pervasive and the support of all beings. कर्म or action is also universal. It manifests itself as different actions of different beings. Svabhāva or nature is that which produces परिणाम or change.
God is both saguṇa and nirguṇa (with and without attributes). He cannot be known except through his own grace. Through his māyāśakti, he can become anything at any time. He is both the material and the efficient cause of this world. He creates the world through his own nature and hence the samavāyi-कारण, the inherent cause. Though he exists everywhere in his tripartite nature as being, चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् and bliss, their manifestation in the created universe differs. Matter reflects only the being aspect (‘sat’), the souls reflect the चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् also (‘cit’) whereas as ब्रह्मन्, he manifests all the three fully.
Though unmanifest and transcendent in his own nature, by creating the world through his will, he becomes manifest and an object of comprehension. Since this world is a manifestation of ब्रह्मन्, it is never destroyed but is only withdrawn into him at his will.
The jīvas or individual souls come out of अक्षर ब्रह्मन् like sparks from fire. They are eternal parts of ब्रह्मन् and are atomic in size. They are of three classes: puṣṭi, maryāda and pravāha. The first are the chosen ones enjoying the grace of God, and ardently devoted to him. The second study the scriptures, perform the rites prescribed as ordained duties and also cultivate devotion. They attain God in course of time. The last are interested only in the worldly life and hence transmigrate constantly. Some of them, due to satsaṅga or good company, may attain God later.
Vallabha considers भक्ति or devotion as the only means of salvation. By that, the जीव is released from the cycle of birth and death and enjoys the bliss of God in all possible ways.
Vallabha holds that the knower of ब्रह्मन् is absorbed in अक्षर-ब्रह्मन् and not in पुरुषोत्तम. It is only through भक्ति that the latter, the highest aspect, can be attained.
He advocates two forms of भक्ति: maryādā-भक्ति and puṣṭi-भक्ति. The former is formal devotion to be practised as described in the scriptures and has to be cultivated by self-effort. The latter is attained by the grace of God alone, without one’s effort. ‘Puṣṭi’ refers, not to the physical nourishment, but to the spiritual nourishment got by the grace of God. Hence the name ‘puṣṭi-भक्ति’. Consequently, वल्लभ’s system is also called ‘Puṣṭi-mārga.’ Emphasis on the worship of Bālakṛṣṇa, (child कृष्ण) and sevā or service to him, find an important place in the mode of sādhanā taught by him.
Baladeva
Baladeva is an important teacher of the Bengal school of वैष्णविस्म् developed by श्रीकृष्ण चैतन्य (A.

-1533). The philosophy of this school is known as Acintyabhedābheda.
Govindabhāṣya is his commentary on the Brahmasūtras, Siddhāntaratna being another work that expounds this philo-sophy. This school, though deeply indebted to the द्वैत system of Madhva, also differs from it.
According to this school of thought, ब्रह्मन् the highest reality is कृष्ण, विष्णु or Hari. He is the Personal God possessed of infinite auspicious qualities, which are ‘acintya’ or beyond our comprehension. He is ‘nirguṇa’ only in the sense that he is beyond the three guṇas of सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्. The scriptures are the only authority to reveal him.
God has three powers: पराशक्ति (higher power), aparāśakti (lower power) and avidyāśakti (nescience power). Through the first, he becomes the efficient cause, and, through the other two, the material cause. When the latter two powers are manifested in gross forms, the universe of souls and matter arises.
Creation of the world is a spontan-eous act of the Lord. However, he does it as per the karmas of the individual souls.
The individual सोउल् is eternal. It is both knowledge and knower, an enjoyer and an active agent, though not independent. It is atomic in size.
Bhakti is the sole and direct cause of salvation. Though ध्यान or upāsanā (meditation) is one form of भक्ति, it is through premābhakti (intense devotion) that God can be realised. Performance of duties purifies the मिन्द्. Study of the scriptures is an aid in the path of sādhanā. However, it is ultimately by the grace of God alone that he can be realised and salvation attained. The freed सोउल् resides in the same world as the Lord and in his proximity, attains his nature and attributes. However, it retains its separate identity.
Baladeva does not admit of जीवन्मुक्ति or लिबेरतिओन् while living in the body here.
The ब्रह्मसूत्र Literature
Being the basic text of Vedānta, both in its metaphysical and and in its dialectical aspect, the Brahmasūtras has attracted the attention of a host of elite scholars over the centuries. Apart from the direct bhāṣyas by the great ācāryas, several subcommentaries and glosses over them have enriched the ब्रह्मसूत्र literature. In such literature now available to us, the maximum number of works belong to the Advaita school.
On the Śāṅkarabhāṣya, three ṭīkās or subcommentaries are available in full: Bhāmati of Vācaspatimiśra (A.
), Nyāyanirṇaya of आनन्दगिरि (A.

) and Ratnaprabhā of रामानन्द (17th century).
The one by पद्मपाद (A.
), a direct disciple of शङ्कर, called Pañca-pādikā deals with the first four sūtras (
-4) only. This was commentated upon by प्रकाशात्मन् (A.
) in his Pañcapādikā-vivaraṇam. There is a gloss on this called Tattvadīpanam by Akhaṇḍā-नन्द मुनि (A.
), Vivaraṇaprameya-saṅgraha of विद्यारण्य (A.

-1369) wrote a gloss called Tattvaṭīkā.
Apart from his bhāṣya (generally called the Madhvabhāṣya) on the Brahma-sūtras, Madhva wrote the Aṇubhāṣya in verses, giving the gist of the various adhikaraṇas of the work. Rāghavendra-tīrtha (A.

-1671) has written an extensive commentary on this and has named it Tattvamañjarī.
Trivikrama Paṇḍita, a disciple of Madhva, has commented upon the bhāṣya of Madhva. It is called the Tattvadīpikā. Tattvaprakāśika of जयतीर्थ (A.
-1388) and Tātparyacandrikā of Vyāsarāya (A.

) are the other commentaries on the same.
However, the most celebrated work of the द्वैत school of Madhva is the Nyāyasudhā of जयतीर्थ which is a highly dialectical and yet lucid commentary on Madhva’s Anuvyākhyāna, a work elucidating his own commentary on the Brahmasūtras.
Nimbārka’s commentary on the Brahmasūtras, known as the Vedānta-पारिजात-saurabha, has been expounded further by Srīnivāsa (13th cent. A. D.) in his Vedānta-kaustubha which again has been explained further by Keśava Kāśmīrin (15th cent. A. D.) in his Vedānta-कौस्तुभ-prabhā.
The other commentaries which have drawn the attention of the Vedāntic scholars are the Vijñānāmṛta-bhāṣya of विज्ञान-भिक्षु (A.

) and the commentary Sūkṣma on बलदेव’s Govinda-bhāṣya.
Apart from these works mentioned here, there are several other treatises and tracts on the various aspects of Vedānta as interpreted by the numerous schools.
Conclusion
There is no gainsaying the fact that the Vedānta system based chiefly on the Brahmasūtras—which itself is a systematic exposition of the philosophy of the Upaniṣads—has influenced all the important aspects of Hindu religion and culture, including the modern Hindu movements.

Brāhmoism
------------------------------------------
It is the philosophy of the Brahma Samāj, one of the modern reform movements of हिन्दुइस्म्, started by राजा राम्मोहन् रोय् (A.

-1833).
See BRAHMA SAMĀJ for details.

Brahmagupta
------------------------------------------
Brahmagupta was a pioneer in the field of mathematics and अस्त्रोनोम्य्. He was born during A.
in Bhinmal in the Jalore district of Rajasthan. His principal works are Brāhmasphuṭa Siddhānta and Khaṇḍakhādyakaraṇa. The former, composed in A.
, has been commented upon by Caturveda Pṛthūdaka Svāmin (A.

), in detail, probably following the tradition of the original author.
As a mathematician, ब्रह्मगुप्त is famous for his work on cakrīyacaturbhuja or cyclic quadrilaterals. His astronomical writings were well-known in Western India even by A.

.
The length of the year as determined by him is slightly less than what is accepted by most of the astronomical texts.
Bhāskarācārya (A.
-1160), the celebrated astronomer, has described ब्रह्मगुप्त as Gaṇakacakracūḍāmaṇi (the crest-jewel among mathematicians).

brāhma-vivāha
(‘marriage of the brāhma [type]’)
------------------------------------------
Out of the ṣodaśa-सṁस्कारस् or sixteen sacraments recommended in the धर्मशास्त्रस् for the dvijas (the ‘twice-born’) विवाह or मर्रिअगे is considered not only very important but also basic, since all the other sacraments depend on it.
Out of the eight forms of मर्रिअगे listed in the works, the brāhma is the best. It is called ‘brāhma’ since it is sanctioned by the वेदस् (Brahma = the Veda) or, is in accordance with धर्म (Brahma = धर्म), the moral law sanctioned by the holy books and sacred traditions.
In this form of मर्रिअगे, the ड़थेर् of the girl bedecks her with the best of clothes and ornaments and gifts her to a worthy young man, learned in the वेदस् and of good character. Before doing so, the bridegroom is invited and honored properly.
See also SAṀSKĀRAS, ṢOḌAŚASAṀ-SKĀRAS and VIVĀHA.

brahmajñāna
(‘Knowledge of ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
The Vedānta system of philosophy posits ब्रह्मन् (‘the Unlimited One,’ ‘the Infinite One,’ ‘the Absolute’) as the origin of the entire universe including the inanimate nature and the living beings. The universe evolves out of it, is sustained in it and involves back into it. Its essential nature is ‘sat-cit-आनन्द,’ ‘existence-चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्-bliss’. It is uncaused and eternal. It is also the very essence of the human beings. Since the human beings do not know this ब्रह्मन् that is in them or behind them, they are undergoing a lot of suffering caused by the vicious circle of birth-death-rebirth, technically called ‘saṁsāra’. मोक्ष or liberating oneself from the bondage of this सṁसार, is the ultimate goal of life. This मोक्ष can be achieved only by ब्रह्मज्ञान.
Though the word ‘jñāna’ means ‘knowledge,’ ‘brahmajñāna’ does not mean an intellectual understanding of ब्रह्मन्. It is anubhūti or direct experience of Brah-man, not only as the substratum of the entire च्रेअतिओन्, but also as the innermost core of oneself. Once this direct experience comes, there will no more be any identification with the body-मिन्द् complex which alone was responsible for सṁसार.
In order to get this experience, one has to cultivate the साधनचतुष्टय first. (See SĀDHANACATUṢṬAYA for details.) This is to be followed by approaching a competent spiritual preceptor from whom one has to listen (śravaṇa) to the Vedāntic truths, reflect (manana) upon them and meditate (nididhyāsana) upon them. This will ultimately lead to ब्रह्मज्ञान or the direct experience of Brahman—often equated with आत्मन्, the Self—and result in मोक्ष.
See also ĀTMAN, BRAHMAN, JÑĀNA and VEDĀNTA-DARŚANA.

Brahmayāmala
------------------------------------------
The आगमस् and the tantras—a special class of religious literature dealing with the different aspects of शैविस्म् and Śāktāism—have the unique distinction of integrating the non-Vedic local religious cults into the general framework of Vedic हिन्दुइस्म्.
The Yāmalas, belonging to the Śaivā-gama group, have, in all probability, derived their name from the fact of their dealing with both शिव and शक्ति (Yamala = twin, couple) in their works. Out of the eight Yāmalas known to exist, the Brahmayāmala, occupies a very important place. According to one version it is said to consist of 22,100 ślokas or verses.
Īśvara propitiated Lord श्रीकण्ठ, got this knowledge from him and then communicated the same to his spouse, पार्वती or देवी.
The work describes the process of च्रेअतिओन् from सदाशिव through his पराशक्ति (supreme energy).
It also traces the origin of the three srotas or currents of tāntric traditions. They are Dakṣiṇa, Vāma and Madhyama. The Dakṣiṇa-srota is characterised by सत्त्व and hence is called ‘śuddha’. The Vāma-srota has predominance of रजस् and hence is ‘miśra’. The last, the Madhyama-srota, is dominated by तमस् and so, is described as ‘aśeṣa-मल-rañjita’ (fully coloured by impurity).
Some of the gods and sages who promulgated this knowledge of शिव are: ईश्वर, Mahādevī, ब्रह्मा, विष्णु, उशनस्, बृहस्पति, Sanatkumāra and लकुलीश.
The earliest manuscript of the Brahmayāmala available now is preserved in Nepal and has been assigned the date A.

. According to it, the eight Yāmalas were communicated by eight Bhairavas such as Svacchanda, Krodha and others. These Yāmalas indicate great developments in the tāntric sādhanās.
See also ĀGAMAS and TANTRAS.

Brahmādvaita-vāda
(‘the school [that teaches] ब्रह्मन्, the one without a second’)
------------------------------------------
All the schools of Vedānta posit ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute, as the primary reality. However, it is the Advaita Vedānta school of शङ्कर (A.

-820) that considers ब्रह्मन्, not just the primary reality, but as the only reality and that it is ‘advaita,’ ‘the one without a second’. This proposition seems to have been put forward not only as the most essential teaching of the उपनिषद्स्, but also to counter the Śabdādvaita-vāda of the grammar schools which propounded that ‘Śabda’ or the ‘Word’ was the sole origin of the universe.
See also ADVAITA-VEDĀNTA-DARŚANA and SPHOṬAVĀDA.

brāhmaṇācchaṁsin
(‘One who recites after the ब्राह्मण’)
------------------------------------------
Vedic sacrifices like the सोमयाग comprise elaborate rites needing 16 priests in all: the four principal priests, each having three assistants. Brāhmaṇā-cchaṁsin is an assistant of the fourth principal priest called ब्रह्मा.
In the अग्निष्टोम sacrifice (which is a model sacrifice in the सोमयाग group) special recitations called ‘ājya-शस्त्र’ have to be chanted, during the first pressing of the सोम juice. They are four in number. ब्राह्मणाच्छṁसिन् chants the third recitation addressed to इन्द्र.

Brahmabhāga
(‘part [representing] ब्रह्मा’)
------------------------------------------
In the literature connected with हिन्दु तेम्प्लेस्, this word is used in two senses. Firstly, it represents the central part of the plot or the site of the sanctum sanctorum, the outer ones being respectively called दैव, mānuṣa and paiśāca bhāgas (parts pertaining to the gods, human beings and goblins).
Secondly, it refers to the lowest part of the शिवलिङ्ग made of stone, which is square in shape and is embedded in the earth. The middle part which is octagonal and is embedded in the pedestal is called विष्णुभाग. The cylindrical part projecting outside the pedestal is called रुद्रभाग. It is also called as पूजाभाग since पूजा or worship is offered only to this part.

brahmavādinī
(‘the woman who speaks about ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
In the ancient days, women were divided into two classes: the brahma-vādinīs and the sadyovadhūs.
The brahmavādinīs underwent the sacrament of उपनयन, kept the Vedic fires, studied the वेदस् under their own ड़थेर् and lived by begging the ड़ोओद्, also under the parental roof. They had samā-vartana (valedictory rite at the end of the period of Vedic studies) also. They could then marry and settle down in life.
The name ‘brahmavādinī’ seems to have been given due to the fact that the girl could recite (vad = to speak or recite) the वेदस् (Brahma = Veda). It might also have been applied to those women who were interested in discussing about ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute, and perform spiritual practices to realize the same. May be due to this reason that the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (4.5.1) calls मैत्रेयी, wife of the sage याज्ञवल्क्य, as a ‘brahmavādinī’.
‘Sadyovadhūs’ were those who became vadhūs or brides straight-away, (sadyas = at once) on the attainment of puberty, without undergoing the training in the Vedic studies. In their case, the उपनयन ceremony was performed just before मर्रिअगे, as a formality.
The practice of performing उपनयन for women as also teaching them the वेदस्, seems to have disappeared even by the time of the Manusmṛti (composed much earlier than A.

).
The word ब्रह्मवादिनी is sometimes applied to the famous Gayatrīmantra also.

Brahmacāriṇī
(‘unmarried or celibate lady’)
------------------------------------------
Out of the innumerable forms of शक्ति (the Divine मोथेर्) mentioned in the tāntric works, ब्रह्मचारिणी is an aspect of दुर्गा. She is pictured as having two arms carrying the rosary and a holy pot. She is one of the नवदुर्गास् or nine aspects of दुर्गा.
The word brahmācāriṇī may also refer to a girl who had undergone the उपनयन ceremony and was studying the वेदस्, which custom seems to have existed in the earlier Vedic period.
In the modern context, it can refer to an unmarried woman in general, and a woman observing lifelong celibacy in particular.

Brāhmaṇagītā
(‘song of the ब्राह्मण’)
------------------------------------------
The Bhagavadgītā became a model for the later generation of writers of didactical literature. Out of several such gītās produced by them, the Brāhmaṇagītā is also one. Actually it is an integral part of a bigger and more well-known work, the Anugītā.
The Brāhmaṇagītā comprises the chapters 20 to 34 (15 chapters; 325 verses) of the Āśvamedhikaparva, the fourteenth book of the epic Mahābhārata.
The wife of a ब्राह्मण approached her husband with an anxious query as to what would happen to her after death since she found him to have abandoned all the actions prescribed in the scriptures and since that would affect her future life also. The ब्राह्मण, who was actually an enlightened person, and hence who had transcended all such actions, started teaching her spiritual wisdom in order to uplift her मिन्द्.
The teaching is couched in a highly symbolical language and often needs expla-nations.
The subjects dealt with may, very briefly, be summarised as follows: superiority of मिन्द् and speech over the other organs, importance of the five prāṇas or vital airs in the body, supremacy of the Lord, who resides in all beings as the अन्तर्यामिन् or the indweller, stories of परशुराम and the king अम्बरीष, and teaching about the क्षेत्रज्ञ or the Self.

Brahmasiddhi
(‘establishment [of the nature of] ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
The Brahmasiddhi of मण्डन मिश्र (A.
) is one of the four major independent treatises of Advaita Vedānta belonging to the Siddhi-group. The other three are: Naiṣkarmyasiddhi of सुरेश्वर (A.
), Iṣṭasiddhi of विमुक्तात्मन् (A.
) and Advaitasiddhi of मधुसूदन सरस्वती (A.

).
The traditional view that मण्डन मिश्र and सुरेश्वर were one and the same person has not been accepted by scholars of repute in the field.
The work is in four chapters: Brahmakāṇḍa, Tarkakāṇḍa, Niyogakāṇḍa and Siddhikāṇḍa. It is in the form of verses (kārikā) and long annotations (vṛtti). Out of the four commentaries said to have been written, that of Śaṅkhapāṇi has been traced and utilised by the savants interested in it.
In the Brahmakāṇḍa, nature of ब्रह्मन् is discussed. The Tarkakāṇḍa discusses questions regarding perception and whether ‘difference’ can be perceived at all. The Niyogakāṇḍa—the longest of the four chapters—refutes certain views of the Mīmāṁsā school. The Siddhikāṇḍa, the shortest, tries to show that the Upaniṣadic texts treat this world of multiplicity as an appearance due to अविद्या or इग्नोरन्चे.
The Advaita Vedānta as propounded here differs from that of शङ्कर in certain respects. Yet, it is considered as an important handbook of Advaita.
See also MAṆḌANA-MIŚRA.

brahmanirvāṇa
(‘getting merged in ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
The Hindu scriptures posit मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् from transmigratory existence as the ultimate goal of life. According to some Vedāntic works, this is attained when the जीव or the individual सोउल् gets merged in ब्रह्मन् or परमात्मन्, the Absolute or the Supreme सोउल्.
Nirvāṇa means getting extinguished like a burning lamp being blown out. When the little or the individual self (jīvātman) extinguishes itself into ब्रह्मन् the Absolute, losing its separate identity and becoming merged in ब्रह्मन्, it is brahmanirvāṅa. Another example that expresses the same idea is the merging of the rivers into the ocean.
Brahmanirvāṇa or मोक्ष can be attained through ज्ञान (knowledge) and भक्ति (devotion).
This word seems to be peculiar only to the Bhagavadgītā (vide 2.72; 5.24-26).

Brahmavidyā Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is one of the minor उपनिषद्स् belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. It is a fairly large work of 110 ślokas or verses in the anuṣṭubh meter. The प्रणव or ओङ्कार as also the Haṁsamantra (so’haṁ haṁsaḥ) are the main topics dealt with. However, the several details that are given, concerning the various aspects of meditation on these two mantras, make the work quite recondite.
The Upaniṣad starts with an exposition of प्रणव, its four parts and contem-plations connected with them. Just as the sound of a gong or a bell, made of bell-metal, gradually gets attenuated, finally merging into the infinite sound or infinite silence, the मिन्द् of a योगि who utters the प्रणव (Oṁ), lengthening it over sixteen mātrās or instants of time, simultaneously concentrating his मिन्द् on that sound, also gets dissolved in ब्रह्मन्, the final goal of प्रणव-जप.
Haṁsavidyā is the next topic taken up. The words ‘haṁ’ and ‘saḥ’ represent the jīvātman (the individual self) and Parmātman or ब्रह्मन् (the Supreme Self) respectively. The natural breathing process of inhalation and exhalation should be mentally connected with the two words ‘haṁ’ and ‘saḥ’. Then the process of breathing itself gets converted into जप (repetition of divine name) ultimately resulting in the experience of the unity of the two. This is Haṁsavidyā.
After stressing that the आत्मन् can be known only through the śruti (the scripture or the वेदस्) and the आचार्य (spiritual preceptor), the Upaniṣad goes on to describe three types of ācāryas—the codaka, the bodhaka and the mokṣada. Codaka is actually the वेदस् which impel a person to take to the spiritual path. The bodhaka is the teacher who teaches the disciple, ‘Thou art That.’ Mokṣada (giver of लिबेरतिओन्) is the Lord himself, since it is only he that can give मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्.
Here, the Upaniṣad declares that it is in the heart alone that one realises this ‘Haṁsa’ or the Lord who is the indwelling spirit.
The work concludes with a long, highly poetical, soliloquy by the knower of the Self, the gist of which is that he exists in all and is all.
See also UPANIṢADS.

Brahmaloka
(‘the world of ब्रह्मा’)
------------------------------------------
The state of a human being before birth and after death has always been a mystery to us, though the various religions of the world have offered their own explanations.
According to the उपनिषद्स् and other allied scriptures, three destinies are possible for a human being: to be reborn here, to go to the पितृलोक or the world of manes and to go to the ब्रह्मलोक or सत्यलोक, the abode of ब्रह्मा.
The path to the पितृलोक lies through the पितृयान or दक्षिणायन or Dhūmādi-mārga, the path of smoke.
The path to the ब्रह्मलोक lies through the देवयान or उत्तरायण or Arcirādimārga, the path of light.
The ब्रह्मलोक, also known as the सत्यलोक, is the final destination of those who have purified themselves by austerities and meditation. They do not return to this mundane existence. They will be there till the end of the कल्प or the cycle of च्रेअतिओन्. When the ब्रह्मलोक too gets dissolved in the Supreme ब्रह्मन्, they will also get merged in It. This is called क्रममुक्ति or gradual लिबेरतिओन् as against sadyomukti or instant लिबेरतिओन्.
The पुराणस् describe ब्रह्मलोक as the highest of the fourteen worlds, six being above this earth and seven, below. The denizens of this ब्रह्मलोक are said to be completely free from all passions and limitations of the physical body, unlike here.
Sometimes, the two worlds below ब्रह्मलोक, viz., the जनलोक and the तपोलोक, are also classed with the ब्रह्मलोक and called as such.
See also DEVAYĀNA and PITṚYĀNA.

brahmāṇḍa
(‘the egg of ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
How this world in which we live and move and have our being, has been created, has always remained a mystery to the human मिन्द्. The Hindu sages have always felt that only the śāstra or the revealed Word, can solve this mystery. However, the accounts of च्रेअतिओन् given in the वेदस्, the उपनिषद्स्, the smṛtis and the पुराणस् are so different—though there are also some common points—that it becomes rather difficult to take as authoritative any one account. That is why commentators on these works stress the point that the main purport of all these works is to point towards God, the creator and the need to know him.
According to the Manusmṛti (1.7-13) Svayambhū, the Self-existent Being, desi-rous of creating the world, brought out water from himself. He laid the seed over it which developed into a golden egg from which he himself was born as ब्रह्मा, the Creator. This golden egg is called ब्रह्माण्ड. ब्रह्मा (also called Hiraṇya-garbha) split it into halves and constructed svargaloka (heaven), भूलोक (earth) and अन्तरिक्ष (the intervening space). In some works, the number of worlds created is listed as fourteen.

brahmakṛcchra
(‘kṛcchra [connected with] brahma’)
------------------------------------------
The concept of sin (pātaka, पाप, agha, enas) is as old as the Ṛgveda itself. Later literature like the smṛtis and the dharmaśastras have dealt with it in great detail. Among the several remedies, austerities of a particular class are given the general name ‘kṛcchra.’ The word means ‘that which cuts, causes pain and suffering.’
Of the several kṛcchras mentioned, ब्रह्मकृच्छ्र is also one. It is difficult to say what exactly the word ‘brahma’ connotes here. Out of the several secondary meanings of the word, ‘tapas’ (austerity) and ‘bhogatyāga’ (renunciation of objects of pleasure) may be more appropriate here. It is an austerity involving the giving up of objects of pleasure.
Brahmakṛcchra is a penance spread over twelve days. It consists in sustaining oneself during that period, by drinking at noon, a little pañcagavya—a preparation of the five products of a cow, viz., milk, curds, ghee, urine and dung—in a temple or a cow-pen, after offering it with mantras in fire. meditation on विष्णु, sleeping near an idol of विष्णु and abjuring certain luxuries like betel leaf and unguents—these are the other disciplines mentioned.
Different kṛcchras are prescribed as expiations for different kinds of sins. The details can be obtained from the relevant धर्मशास्त्रस्.
See also KṚCCHRA.

Brāhmaṇas
(‘[liturgical texts] of ब्रह्मन् or the वेदस्’)
------------------------------------------
The वेदस्, the basic scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म्, are broadly divided into two parts: the Saṁhitās and the ब्राह्मणस्. The latter include the आरण्यकस् and the उपनिषद्स्, though these latter two are also considered as two more parts, different from the Saṁhitās and the ब्राह्मणस्.
Whereas the Saṁhitās comprise the mantras or hymns in praise of the various Vedic deities like अग्नि and इन्द्र, the ब्राह्मणस्, composed in prose, explain the mantras, prescribe their use in sacrifices and also give the know-how of the sacrifices in detail.
Yajñas and yāgas—sacrifices offered into the duly consecrated fire—occupied the central place in Vedic religion. Hence, the need for clear and elaborate instructions to conduct them was keenly felt. And, the ब्राह्मणस् fulfilled that need.
The primary content of the ब्राह्मणस् can be stated as ‘vidhi’ or injunctions concerning the various rites and rituals which form a part of the sacrificial system. It comprises such details as: when to perform a sacrifice, which sacrifice for which purpose, who is the person fit to perform it, which are the various components, what are the mantras to be used, where and how, and so on.
Apart from the vidhis, the ब्राह्मणस् also contain other topics: हेतु, nirukti, stuti or अर्थवाद and आख्यान.
Those portions of the work that provide लोगिच् and reasoning in support of a विधि are called ‘hetu’. Wherever certain words are explained with their etymological derivations, such statements are termed as ‘nirukti’. Stuti or अर्थवाद comprises the statements of praise in support of the injunctions and of derogation, in support of prohibitions. Ākhyānas are stories or narration of ancient incidents interspersed in the body of the ब्राह्मण literature. They are often full of esoteric meanings or philosophical speculations.
The ब्राह्मणस् occupy a very impor-tant place in the Vedic lore. They provided not only the necessary details for the performance of Vedic rites but also the inspiration to sustain them. The various discussions that used to take place during the ब्राह्मण period, concerning the several aspects of the sacrificial religion, gave rise to the Mīmāṁsā system of philosophy.
As in the case of the other ancient Hindu scriptures, it is rather difficult to fix up definitely the date of the ब्राह्मण literature. Whereas the Western Indologists assign the dates 1200 B. C. to A.

, the Indian scholars, basing their arguments mainly on the astronomical data available in the Brāhmaṇas—like the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa—push it back to the period 3000 B.C. to 2000 B.C.
The entire ब्राह्मण literature is in prose. It is the most ancient prose in Sanskrit literature available to us now. The sentences are simple and straight. Long compound words or grammatically intricate structures are practically unknown. Hence, it is much more intelligible to the readers. The absence of archaic words found in the Saṁhitās and the use of many new words give us the impression that the Sanskrit of the ब्राह्मणस् represents a transition stage from the Vedic to the classical Sanskrit.
The ब्राह्मणस् give us an inkling into the contemporary social life too. People were very much devoted to the performance of the sacrifices. Hence they were extensively practised. This naturally led to the brāhmaṇas—members of the first of the four varṇas—occupying the pre-eminent place in the social setup. They were treated practically as gods on earth. However, they had to earn that status through the mastery of the वेदस् and तपस् or austerities.
The वर्ण system—division of the society into four broad groups based on the natural propensities and professions chosen—had become well-established. The क्षत्त्रिय ruler had to submit himself to the guidance and advice of the ब्राह्मणस्. The vaiśyas were devoted to the development of the whole society through their activities of trade, commerce and agriculture. Those who were not capable of the other three vocations contented themselves in living by serving others. They were the शूद्रस्.
Great importance was attached to सत्य and धर्म, truth and righteous behaviour. One who forsook the path of truth was considered unfit for the performance of sacrifices. Slipping into sinful ways would result in a vicious circle, thereby obliging the sinners to commit more heinous sins. Hence it had to be avoided at all costs. Since purity in personal life would conduce to the purity of social life, it was highly regarded and stressed. And, the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् were believed to help the human beings in achieving this goal.
People hankered for progeny, especi-ally for virtuous sons. A chaste woman was always respected.
Each of the four वेदस् has its own ब्राह्मणस्. Since the number of the extant ब्राह्मणस् is rather small compared to what has been mentioned in the गृह्यसूत्रस् and other ancient works, it can safely be surmised that many of them have been lost, perhaps irretrievably.
The ब्राह्मणस् available now, may be listed as follows:
ṚGVEDA
Aitareya Brāhmaṇa and Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa.
YAJURVEDA
Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa and Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.
SĀMAVEDA
Tāṇḍya ब्राह्मण, Ṣaḍviṁśa Brāh-maṇa, Sāmavidhāna Brāhmaṇa, Ārṣeya ब्राह्मण, Daivata ब्राह्मण, सṁहितोपनिषद् ब्राह्मण, Upaniṣad Brāh-maṇa, Vaṁśa Brāhmaṇa and Jaiminīya ब्राह्मण.
ATHARVAVEDA
Gopatha ब्राह्मण.
An idea of the contents of these ब्राह्मणस् can be obtained under the respective titles.

Brahma-vaivarta-purāṇa
------------------------------------------
Modern हिन्दुइस्म्, though rooted in the वेदस् and the Vedānta, is deeply influenced by the पुराणस्, at least on the practical side. The Brahma-vaivarta-purāṇa is one such that is often quoted by the writers of the धर्मशास्त्रस् while dealing with topics like castes, gifts, vratas (religious vows during festival days), descriptions of narakas or hells for transgression of धर्म and so on. The original part of the purāṇa may be ancient. However, the extant edition, as available in print, seems to have evolved over the period A.

-1600.
It is probable that this purāṇa may have acquired this title because it treats this created world as only a vivarta of or an appearance in ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute.
It is a fairly voluminous work comprising 18,000 verses spread over four khaṇḍas or books, the total number of chapters being 276.
The first book called Brahmakhaṇḍa lauds this purāṇa and also gives a gist of the contents of the entire work. It declares that it is Śrī कृष्ण who is the creator of the entire universe and that his world, the गोलोक, is the highest of all the divine abodes, even वैकुण्ठ and कैलास being inferior to it. A detailed account of च्रेअतिओन् which includes the emanation of other deities like नारायण, शङ्कर or शिव, ब्रह्मा and धर्म-पुरुष, as also the goddesses like Mūrti, लक्ष्मी, सरस्वती, दुर्गा and सावित्री is also given. Other topics dealt with in this book include आयुर्वेद, (science of health) worship of शालग्राम (the stone symbol of विष्णु), austerities to be practised by the saṁnyāsins and widows, philosophical teachings concerning the ultimate identity of the जीव (individual सोउल्) with ब्रह्मन् and a description of the गोलोक.
Prakṛtikhaṇḍa, the second book, deals with the mūlaprakṛti or the मोथेर् Nature, who is pictured as the consort of God, forming the left part of his body as it were. She evolves into five goddesses: Rādha and दुर्गा, लक्ष्मी and सरस्वती as also सावित्री. God or पुरुष splits himself into Śrī कृष्ण and नारायण. Later, ब्रह्मा and शिव also emanate from him.
Mūlaprakṛti gives birth to a golden egg from which emerges Mahāvirāṭ, the Cosmic Being. He creates the worlds.
As in the previous khaṇḍa, here also a number of miscellaneous subjects have been dealt with: stories of various female deities including the river-goddesses, worship and meditation concerning Bhūmi or मोथेर् Earth, merits of a bath in the गङ्गा River, importance of the tuḷasī leaves and rules concerning its use, details of the various शालग्राम stones, the well-known story of सावित्री and सत्यवान्, कर्म and its effects, descriptions of narakas or hells, detailed information about the growth of the human foetus in the womb, story of दुर्गा in brief as also some details about her worship.
Next comes Gaṇapatikhaṇḍa. This book deals mainly with the birth and exploits of गणपति and षण्मुख, the two sons of शिव and पार्वती. The story of परशुराम (the राम of the battle-axe) is also an important part of this section. There are quite a few beautiful hymns in praise of गणपति.
Śrī-कृष्ण-janma-khaṇḍa, the last book, is also the biggest. Though the story of कृष्ण follows the one given in the Bhāgavata, the amorous deeds of राधा and कृष्ण are portrayed prominently. Stories of अम्बरीष and Durvāsa, अष्टावक्र and Śrī राम also find a place. A variety of topics like the evil omens indicated by bad द्रेअम्स्, duties of the people belonging to the four varṇas, special code of conduct for the widows, foods fit and unfit for consuming, description of कलियुग or the Iron Age, greatness of the country of Bhārata and the science of architecture are also included at appropriate places.
The last chapter of this book gives a list of eighteen major पुराणस् along with the total number of verses in each of them.
A special feature of this purāṇa is that it gives several important mantras (esoteric formulae) as also their usage.
See also PURĀṆAS.

brahmapura
(‘city of ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
This word has been used in the उपनिषद्स् in several senses. Just as a city, (pura = city) full of people and various goods, supplies the wants of the king, this body of several limbs and sense-organs, supplies the needs of ब्रह्मन् who resides in it in the form of the जीव or the indi-vidual सोउल्. Hence it is called ‘brahmapura’ or ‘the city of ब्रह्मन्’ (vide Chāndogya Upaniṣad

).
Sometimes the word is applied to the ‘lotus of the heart’ (hṛdayapuṇḍarīka—the psychic heart, where meditation is practised) since it ‘houses’ ब्रह्मन्; i.e., ब्रह्मन् is realised there by the practice of meditation on it, there. (vide Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad

Brahma-Samāj
------------------------------------------
a) The background
During the latter part of the eighteenth century and the early part of the nineteenth, the Hindu society was in a state of turmoil. English एदुचतिओन् and Christian culture imposed on a subject nation by the British rulers and their comrades, the Christian Church, had had a devastating effect on the minds of the younger generation. They were fast losing faith in their मोथेर् religion, हिन्दुइस्म्, as also in the Hindu values of life and culture. It was at this critical juncture that three renaissance movements sprang forth from the bosom of हिन्दुइस्म्. The Brahma Samāj (also spelt as Brāhmo Samāj) was the earliest in the series, followed by the Ārya Samāj and the Ramakrishna Movement.
b) A Brief History
Rājā Rāmmohan Roy (A.

-1833), the founder of the Brahma Samāj was born in a village in the Hoogly district of Bengal in 1772. Not much is known of his early life. He settled down in Calcutta in 1814. By the time he came into prominence he was already a good scholar in Sanskrit, Persian and Arabic languages. Later on, he mastered the English language also. Being dissatisfied with the various Hindu religious practices of his times like idol worship, छिल्द्-मर्रिअगे and सती (burning of widows on the funeral pyres of their husbands) as also the problems of young widows, and, after studying deeply the धर्मशास्त्रस् (Hindu law-books) he came to the conclusion that these were later accretions responsible for the decadence of the Hindu society. With a view to reforming the Hindu social values and practices and take them back to their original source, viz., the उपनिषद्स्, he established the Brahma Samāj on August 20, 1828. Scholars of repute like Rāmacandra विद्या-vāgīśa, Utsavānanda Vidyāvāgīśa and Tārācandra Cakravartī were his collaborators in this work. He succeeded in building a permanent home for it in 1830.
When he passed away in 1833, there was a temporary setback to the movement. However, the entry of Dvārakānāth Ṭhākūr and his son Devendranāth Ṭhākūr (father of the famous poet, Rabindranath Tagore) rejuvenated the movement, the contribution of the latter being much more.
It was the ‘Maharṣi’ Devendranāth Ṭhākūr (as he was popularly known) that introduced the study of the उपनिषद्स् and allied literature through a formal seat of learning which he named as ‘Tattvabodhinī सभा’. This सभा attracted the attention of the elite and its membership swelled. He also composed the text of the oath that every member of the Samāj had to take at the time of admission into it and framed a code of conduct to be followed by all.
Keśavacandra Sen (A.

-1884), the younger contemporary of the महर्षि Devendranāth was the next important leader of this movement. He became the आचार्य or minister when he was hardly twentyfour. He paid much greater attention to the propagation of the Brāhmo ideals and social reforms. He started the Vāmābodhinī, a Bengali journal meant exclusively for women as also the English journal Indian Mirror. He toured the country extensively, delivering lectures and opened a branch—the Veda Samāja—at Madras in 1864. Serious differences with his mentor Devendranāth led to his parting of ways and establishing his own organization, the ‘Brahma Samāj of India’ (‘Bhārat-Varṣīya Brahma Samāj’) in 1866. The parent body came to be known as the ‘Ādi Brahma Samāj’. Whereas the latter considered the Brahma Samāj movement as an integral part of हिन्दुइस्म्, the doors of the former were open to the non-Hindus also. केशवचन्द्र सेन्’s Samāj suffered a serious setback when Paṇḍit Śivnāth Śāstrī got separated from him and established the ‘Sādhāraṇ Brahma Samāj’ in 1878. Keśav’s marrying his minor daughter to the prince of Cooch Bihar, against the rules of the Samāj which he himself had framed or endorsed, was one of the main reasons for this schism.
After केशवचन्द्र सेन्, there being no leaders of comparable eminence, the influence of the Brāhmo movement gradually waned and it is now almost a spent force.
c) The Creed and the Rituals
According to the famous Trust Deed of the Brahma Samāj created by राजा राम्मोहन् रोय्, इमगे wओर्स्हिप् in any form is to be totally abjured, though its practice by others shall not be reviled. It accepts the philosophy of the उपनिषद्स् but rejects Vedic ritualism and the worship of several deities current in the Hindu society. It believes in one God, ब्रह्मन्, the formless Supreme Reality. It lays great emphasis on the cultivation of moral virtues and advocates social reforms like एदुचतिओन् of women, remarriage of widows, equal share for women in parental property, toning down of the caste distinctions and so on.
The प्रतिज्ञा or the oath to be taken by every member at the time of admission into the Samāj, as introduced by Devendra-nāth, emphasised the need to repeat the Gāyatrīmantra before ड़ोओद्, to give up इमगे wओर्स्हिप् in any form, to pay the prescribed subscription to the Samāj regularly and to shape one’s life according to the principles of Vedānta advocated by the founder.
Devendranāth also systematised the rites to be performed at birth, at the time of naming the child, during मर्रिअगे and at the time of death—all in consonance with the basic principles of the Samāj.
The service conducted during the weekly meetings generally consisted of Vedic chanting behind a screen, readings from the उपनिषद्स्, discourses and prayers. Singing of devotional songs was added later on by केशवचन्द्र सेन्.
d) Epilogue
The Brahma Samāj rendered useful service to the Hindu society by popularising social reforms like the abolition of the practice of the सती, by preventing चोन्वेर्सिओन् of the Hindus to Christianity and by rousing the orthodox Hindus to revive their ancient religion. However, its refusal to recognize the accepted canon of Hindu scriptures and certain deep-rooted beliefs like the faith in the Avatāras or incarnations of God, undermined its credibility in the eyes of the common Hindu masses. This may be the chief reason for its listless existence now.

Brahmaputra
(‘son of ब्रह्मा’)
------------------------------------------
The ब्रह्मपुत्र is one of the major rivers of India.
There are two mythological accounts about its origin: Amoghā, the wife of the sage Śāntanu conceived by the grace of ब्रह्मा the creator and gave birth to a son. He was named as ‘Brahmaputra’. He was placed in the midst of four mountains by his ड़थेर्. He then assumed the form of a large mass of water where gods and heavenly maidens started taking bath. It came to be known as ‘Brahmakuṇḍa’. It then started flowing as a river.
When परशुराम was ordered by his ड़थेर् जमदग्नि to kill his own मोथेर्, he executed it with his axe. Since it was a heinous act, the axe got stuck in his hand. To get it out, he started on a पिल्ग्रिमगे. When he came to the small lake, now known as Paraśurāmakuṇḍa (25 kms. [15 miles] to the north of Teza in the Lomita district of Arunachal Pradesh), he broke one of the hills surrounding it to release the water for the benefit of mankind. This became the river ब्रह्मपुत्र and the axe came out there by indicating that he was absolved of the sin.
Brahmaputra originates in south-western Tibet, and is called Yarlung or Tsangpo. After flowing for 1300 kms. (800 miles) it bends to the south and enters India. For some distance it is called the Siang river. It falls to the plains at Pasighat in Arunachal Pradesh. It is interesting to note that it changes colour here, every half an hour. As the river Dibang and Lohit join it, it acquires the name ब्रह्मपुत्र and enters Assam. Passing through the towns of Dibrugarh, Nehamati, Tezim and Guwahati, it finally joins the Padmā river, the easternmost branch of the गङ्गा. This combined stream flows into Bangladesh where it joins the river Meghanā. It then empties into the Bay of Bengal. The total length of the river is 2,850 kms. (1800 miles). The average depth of the river is 38 meters (124 ft.), the maximum being 120 metres (380 ft.).
The ब्रह्मपुत्र valley is associated with lores from the Mahābhārata as also with Śaivite traditions.
The famous Kāmākhya temple is situated on its bank, about 2 kms. away, near Guwahati. The banks of this river are dotted with dense forests and tribal settlements.
During monsoon, floods are very common.
The river is mainly used for transpor- tation and navigation.

Brahmakumārīs
------------------------------------------
A handful of men and women living in Hyderabad (in Sind, now in Pakistan) started a group, ‘Om Maṇḍali’ by name, for spiritual studies and meditation in A.
. One year later, it was shifted to Karachi where it continued up to A.

.
Dada Lekhraj Kriplani (A.
-1969) a respected and wealthy member of this community, started experiencing a series of visions in A.

which transformed his life. He wound up his jewellery business and dedicated the rest of his life for spiritual pursuits.
He came to be known as Brahma Bābā among his followers.
In A.

, he formed a Managing Committee of eight young women and in the next year, he surrendered all his property to a Trust administered by them.
These ladies came to be known as ब्रह्मकुमारीस् and became the progenitors of the movement in that name. Though this is primarily run by women, men too (known as Brahmakumāras) participate in its activities.
The community shifted to Mount Abu (in Rajasthan, India) in A.

and built its Head Quarters there. Its official name is “Brahma Kumaris’ World Spiritual University” (BKWSU). It is managed by the Administrative Head, a Governing Board and a Management Committee.
At the Headquarters there are three campuses: Madhuban, Gyan Sarovar and Shantivan. There is also a recreational park and the Global Hospital and Research Centre.
These Campuses have several buildings including auditoria and living quarters.
Meditation techniques called Rāja योग are taught in this institution.
The organisation claims to have several centres in India and abroad.

brahmavāda
(‘the philosophy [that propounds] ब्रह्मन्’)
------------------------------------------
The Bhāgavata occupies a pre-eminent place not only among the पुराणस् but also among the general scriptures of हिन्दुइस्म् on its own. It is a gospel of divine life and is not a textbook of systematic philosophy.
Its teaching has a theoretical as well as a practical aspect. The former is known as ब्रह्मवाद and the latter as भागवत-धर्म.
The essence of ब्रह्मवाद is that ब्रह्मन् or आत्मन् is the only Absolute Reality. The whole universe, including our body, मिन्द् and ego, is only an expression in name and form of that ब्रह्मन्. However, this view differs from pantheism in that ब्रह्मन् does not exhaust himself in the manifestation of this universe. He is neither limited nor affected in any way by the phenomenal universe. And yet, he is both immanent and transcendent.
